blocks.purpose: Defines the complete-sentence rule (subject + verb + complete thought) with prerequisite bullets naming subjects, verbs, and clauses.

data.anchor: A complete sentence needs a subject, a finite verb, and a complete thought — if any one is missing, it is a fragment.
prerequisites: A subject is who or what the sentence is about: 'The goalie saved it.' Subject: the goalie.
A finite verb is a verb that changes with the subject and shows time: 'she runs' works, but 'running fast' alone has no subject and no set time.
A clause is any group of words with its own subject and verb. Some clauses can stand alone (independent); some cannot (dependent).
A thought is complete when a listener isn't left waiting for more — 'When the whistle blew' leaves you asking 'then what?'

data.footnote: Both errors are sentence-wannabes: one has too little, one has too much.

items.label: Has all three parts
items.text: Subject + finite verb + complete thought.
items.example: We lost the game.

items.label: Stands alone
items.text: You can read it by itself and no part feels unfinished.
items.example: The referee checked the replay.

items.label: One independent clause = fine
items.text: A single clause that could stand alone is a full sentence.

rightColumn.heading: What it is NOT (the two errors)

items.label: Fragment
items.text: Missing a subject, a verb, or the end of the thought — often a dependent clause or phrase standing alone.
items.example: Because the buzzer beat us. (What happened?)

items.label: Run-on (fused)
items.text: Two or more independent clauses smashed together with no punctuation at all.
items.example: We lost the game our bench was tired.

items.label: Comma splice
items.text: A run-on where only a comma stands between two full clauses — a comma isn't strong enough to join them.
items.example: We lost the game, our bench was tired.

blocks.purpose: Numbered procedure for fixing a run-on: locate clauses, decide the relationship, choose period, semicolon, or comma+FANBOYS.

steps.detail: Example: 'We lost the game our bench was tired.' Clue: two subject-verb pairs with nothing (or only a comma) between them.
steps.label: 1. Find the clauses
steps.text: Underline each subject-verb pair. If you find two or more independent clauses joined with no punctuation or only a comma, you have a run-on.

steps.detail: The relationship decides the punctuation: a sharp break, a close link, or a explained-by/but link.
steps.label: 2. Ask how the ideas relate
steps.text: Are they two separate statements, two closely related thoughts, or is one the cause, time, or contrast for the other?

steps.detail: 'We lost the game. Our bench was tired.'
steps.label: 3a. Sharp break → period
steps.text: Use a period (or question mark) to make two sentences when the ideas stand on their own.

steps.detail: 'We lost the game; our bench was tired.'
steps.label: 3b. Close link → semicolon
steps.text: Use a semicolon when the second clause follows closely from the first and no connecting word fits.

steps.detail: 'We lost the game, and our bench was tired.' Or: 'Our bench was tired because we had no subs.'
steps.label: 3c. Logical link → comma + FANBOYS or subordinating word
steps.text: Join with a comma plus and, but, or, nor, for, so, or yet — or use because, when, although, since, if, or that to make one clause depend on the other.

But a sentence starting with an independent clause that ENDS with a dependent clause is complete — the dependent clause just answers 'why.' The trap is assuming every 'because' chunk is a fragment.

blocks.purpose: Define the core idea — sentence patterns are choices that control emphasis and rhythm — with plain definitions of periodic, cumulative, and balanced sentences as the prerequisite terms.

data.anchor: A sentence's pattern is a choice about what the reader gets first — and what they get first is what they feel most.
prerequisites: Every sentence needs a subject and a verb; that unit is called a main clause (or independent clause).
Words that add detail — phrases and describing clauses — are called modifiers.
When two clauses or phrases share the same grammatical shape, the sentence is parallel.
A pattern is not grammar-correct vs. incorrect; all three patterns below are correct, but each creates a different rhythm and emphasis.

blocks.purpose: Place a periodic sentence beside a cumulative version of the same idea so the learner sees how emphasis shifts from suspense to elaboration.

data.footnote: Neither pattern is better. Periodic builds suspense and lands the point at the end; cumulative leads with the point and lets the detail pile up.

items.label: Shape
items.text: Modifiers and setup come first; the main clause waits until the very end, so the reader hangs on every word.
items.example: After months of practice, worn out but stubborn, she finally scored.

items.label: Effect
items.text: Suspense and a strong final punch. The reader cannot relax until the sentence finishes.

items.label: Shape
items.text: The main clause opens the sentence; modifiers are added on afterward like freight cars behind the engine.
items.example: She finally scored, after months of practice, worn out but stubborn, in the last minute of the game.

items.label: Effect
items.text: A clear, immediate point plus richness. The reader gets the news right away, then gets the texture.

blocks.purpose: Clear up the technical terms (independent clause, modifier, parallelism, main clause) that the pattern definitions rely on.

data.footer: Tap each underlined term to see what it really means — the pattern names will make much more sense with these four words unlocked.
data.heading: Decode the terms behind the patterns
data.sentence: A sentence pattern works by deciding where the {mainClause} sits and how the {modifiers} are arranged, which requires {independentClause} to be complete and often uses {parallelism} to make halves match.

terms.definition: A group of words with its own subject and verb that could stand alone as a complete sentence. The main clause is the one the sentence is really about.
terms.hint: "She scored" is a complete main clause; "after months of practice" is not.
terms.label: main clause

terms.definition: Words or phrases that add description or detail but cannot stand alone, like "worn out but stubborn" or "in the last minute."
terms.hint: Modifiers dress up the sentence; they are not the sentence's spine.
terms.label: modifiers

terms.definition: A clause with a subject and a verb that expresses a complete thought and can be a sentence by itself.
terms.hint: If it starts with a word like "because," "when," or "although," it cannot stand alone.
terms.label: independent clause

terms.definition: Repeating the same grammatical shape in two or more parts of a sentence, so the parts mirror each other.
terms.hint: "Practice builds confidence; confidence builds success." Both halves: subject + verb + object.
terms.label: parallelism

blocks.purpose: Anchor the three patterns to an everyday physical comparison — a delayed punch, a rolling snowball, and a seesaw — so the abstract shapes stick.

analogies.because: Both hold the payoff until the moment of maximum pressure, then release it.
analogies.everydayScene: A boxer fakes left, steps back, and holds the punch — the longer the wind-up, the harder the payoff lands at the end.
analogies.mapsTo: A periodic sentence holds back the main clause until the very end.

analogies.because: Both start with a clear core and grow by attaching material on afterward, keeping the beginning in view.
analogies.everydayScene: One small snowball rolls downhill and picks up layer after layer of snow, growing bigger as it goes, while the core stays in front the whole way.
analogies.mapsTo: A cumulative sentence starts with the main idea and keeps adding modifiers after it.

analogies.because: Both work only when the two sides are built the same way and carry equal weight.
analogies.everydayScene: Two kids of equal weight sit on opposite ends of a seesaw and it hangs perfectly level — change the shape or weight on one side and it tips.
analogies.mapsTo: A balanced sentence mirrors two equal ideas in parallel structure.

data.bridgeStatement: Three sentences, three physical feelings: wait, pile, tip.
data.rule: Periodic sentences delay the main clause; cumulative sentences lead with it and keep adding; balanced sentences mirror two equal ideas.

checks.answer: Periodic — the main clause lands at the end, building suspense

checks.hint: Find the main clause's subject and verb. Do they arrive at the very end?

Cumulative — the main idea comes first, with detail added after
Balanced — two equal ideas mirror each other
Fragment — the sentence is missing a subject or verb

checks.prompt: Why is "Writing clarifies thinking, and thinking sharpens writing" effective as a balanced sentence?
checks.answer: Its two halves share the same grammatical shape, giving both ideas equal weight
checks.rationale: Both halves use subject + verb + object, so the parallel shape gives the two ideas equal weight — that is what balance means.
checks.hint: What makes the two sides of the sentence feel equal?
choices: It surprises the reader by delivering the main idea first
Its two halves share the same grammatical shape, giving both ideas equal weight
It delays the main clause so the reader feels suspense

checks.hint: Is there any complete subject-verb unit anywhere in the sentence?
choices: It is a fragment — it never delivers a subject and verb
It is a run-on — two independent clauses are joined by only a comma
It is a correct periodic sentence

blocks.purpose: Define rhetorical grammar: grammar choices (word order, clause type, sentence shape) selected for effect on the reader, with prerequisites on subjects, verbs, and clauses.

data.anchor: Rhetorical grammar means choosing your grammatical structures — word order, clause type, and sentence shape — on purpose, for the effect they create in the reader.
prerequisites: You can find the subject and the verb in any sentence.
You can tell a complete sentence from a fragment by checking for a subject, a verb, and a finished thought.
You know that a run-on is two complete sentences joined without correct punctuation or a connecting word.
You can identify a subordinate clause — one that starts with a word like 'because,' 'although,' or 'if' — and tell it apart from a main clause.

items.example: 'The research is clear. Plain and simple.' — short, deliberate, punchy.

items.example: 'If we do not act now, the forest will be gone.'
items.label: Periodic build-up
items.text: A sentence that delays the main point to the end so the reader leans forward waiting for it.

items.example: 'Silence, never again.'
items.label: Fronted phrase
items.text: A key phrase moved to the start of the sentence so the reader meets it first.

items.example: 'We came, we saw, we stayed.'
items.label: Parallel structure
items.text: Matching grammatical forms repeated to build rhythm and credibility.

items.example: 'I missed the bus I was late for class.'
items.label: Accidental fragment or run-on
items.text: A fragment that drops a needed subject or verb by mistake, or a run-on that jams two sentences together without punctuation.

items.example: 'The the result was very unique in every way.'
items.label: Rule-breaking
items.text: Breaking grammar rules without a purpose, which reads as carelessness rather than style.

items.label: Longer is stronger

blocks.purpose: Warns about the top errors: fragments that just read as mistakes, run-ons, and parallelism broken mid-list, with non-examples of each.

cautions.detail: A fragment only works as a rhetorical choice when the reader can tell it is deliberate — usually because it is very short, follows a complete sentence, and clearly echoes it. A stray phrase on its own just reads as a typo.
cautions.rightExample: The storm passed by morning. Then silence.
cautions.title: Deliberate vs. accidental fragments
cautions.wrongExample: Walking home because the bus was late.
cautions.exampleNote: The right example is two words the reader instantly understands as deliberate. The wrong one looks like a missing piece.

cautions.detail: A run-on occurs when two or more complete sentences are joined with no punctuation or connector. Blurred structure blurs persuasion: the reader cannot tell which idea to weigh.
cautions.rightExample: The plan was bold. It was also risky.
cautions.title: Run-ons kill impact
cautions.wrongExample: The plan was bold it was also risky.
cautions.exampleNote: The run-on makes both ideas run together; the corrected version gives each its own punch.

cautions.detail: In a list, once you start a pattern (for example, all -ing verbs), every item must keep it. One mismatched item breaks the rhythm and the reader's trust.
cautions.rightExample: We came, we saw, we listened.
cautions.title: Parallelism broken mid-list
cautions.wrongExample: We came, we saw, listening to every word.
cautions.exampleNote: Keep the same form for every item in the series.

cautions.detail: Rhetorical grammar bends conventions on purpose, not by accident. Before you break a rule, make sure you can build the plain, correct sentence first — then decide that the broken version works harder.
cautions.rightExample: Wrinkled. Stained. Perfect anyway. (three fragments with no preceding full sentence)
cautions.title: Don't transfer 'stylistic' to every context
cautions.wrongExample: Using fragments in a lab report conclusion to sound dramatic.
cautions.exampleNote: In formal reporting, complete sentences are the effect you want.

data.flagIntro: Deliberate grammar choices work only when the reader senses they are deliberate. These three errors are the ways 'artistic license' turns into an actual mistake.

blocks.purpose: Targets the #1 mistake — mistaking any short sentence for an intentional fragment — and reveals why the intuition failed.

data.anchor: Keep active and passive voice consistent within a sentence and paragraph unless you have a specific reason to shift.
prerequisites: Voice describes whether the subject acts (active) or is acted upon (passive). In 'The dog chased the cat,' the dog acts: active voice. In 'The cat was chased by the dog,' the cat receives the action: passive voice.
Active voice usually reads more direct and energetic; passive voice puts the spotlight on the receiver of the action.
You find passive voice by looking for a form of 'be' plus a past participle: was chased, is thrown, will be finished.
A shift is a change in grammatical pattern in the middle of a sentence or a closely connected group of sentences.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side 'What voice is' vs. 'What mood is' so learners separate the two ideas that are commonly confused.

data.footnote: Voice is about who acts; mood is about how the sentence speaks. Both can shift, and both shifts can be wrong.

items.label: The relationship of subject to action
items.text: Voice answers: is the subject doing the action or receiving it?
items.example: Active: 'She lifted the box.' Passive: 'The box was lifted.'

items.label: What it affects
items.text: Voice changes who the sentence seems to focus on, and how direct it sounds.

items.label: What it does NOT change
items.text: Voice does not change what kind of sentence it is. Both examples above are statements.

items.label: The sentence's attitude toward the action
items.text: Mood answers: is the writer stating a fact, giving an order, or talking about something wished, demanded, or imagined?
items.example: Indicative: 'The door is open.' Imperative: 'Open the door.' Subjunctive: 'I demand that the door be open.'

items.label: The three moods you need
items.text: Indicative states facts and questions. Imperative gives commands. Subjunctive covers wishes, demands, suggestions, and unreal situations.

items.label: What it does NOT change
items.text: Mood is not the same as tone. Tone is the writer's attitude; mood here is a grammatical category.

sections.heading: Complete sentences, fragments, and run-ons
paragraphs: A complete sentence needs three things: a subject, a finite verb, and a complete thought. A finite verb shows tense — walked, is, will arrive — and can act as the main verb of the clause. If any of the three pieces is missing, you have a fragment.

Fragments come in a few flavors. "Ran across the field" has no subject. "The player sprinting down the sideline" has no finite verb (sprinting is an -ing form, which cannot be a main verb by itself). "Because the storm arrived" is a subordinate-clause fragment: it starts with a subordinating word, so the thought is incomplete even though a subject and verb are there.

A run-on (also called a fused sentence) joins two independent clauses with no punctuation at all: "The game ended we went home." A comma splice is a run-on that someone tried to fix with a comma alone: "The game ended, we went home." A comma is not strong enough to join two complete clauses on its own.

You can fix a run-on four ways: use a period or question mark to split it; use a semicolon between closely related clauses; use a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so); or turn one clause into a dependent one with a subordinating word like because, when, although, or that.

sections.heading: Word order and sentence patterns
paragraphs: Word order controls emphasis. The same ideas read differently depending on where you put the main clause — first, last, or in the middle — because readers pay the most attention to where the sentence starts and where it lands.

A periodic sentence saves the main clause for the end to build suspense and deliver a punch: "After hours of waiting, through the rain and the crowd, the train finally came." A cumulative sentence does the opposite: it starts with the main clause, then piles on phrases and detail: "The train finally came, after hours of waiting, through the rain, past the crowd." A balanced sentence has two or more parallel parts of similar length and structure, which creates symmetry. Antithesis is a special balanced structure that sets contrasting ideas against each other: "Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country."
The point is not one pattern being better — it is choosing the pattern that matches your purpose: periodic for suspense, cumulative for richness, balanced or antithetical for contrast and punch.

sections.heading: Rhetorical grammar: fragments on purpose
paragraphs: Rhetorical grammar means choosing grammatical structures for their persuasive and stylistic impact. That includes the deliberate stylistic fragment: a piece like "Which changed everything." that you end a paragraph with on purpose. What makes it work is context — it is short by design, it sits next to complete sentences, and it points back at a thought the reader already has. An accidental fragment, like "Running late for practice." in the middle of a body paragraph, just reads like a mistake. Same shape, different intent.

sections.heading: Voice and mood shifts
paragraphs: Voice is about active vs. passive. In an active sentence the subject does the action ("The dog chased the ball"); in a passive one the subject receives it ("The ball was chased by the dog"). Passive voice is fine when the receiver matters more than the doer — but shifting between active and passive inside a sentence or paragraph without a reason is an inappropriate voice shift: "She wrote the essay, and then it was edited by her brother." Fix it by keeping both clauses in one voice: "She wrote the essay, and her brother edited it."

Mood is about the attitude of the verb. Indicative states facts or asks questions ("The doors open at nine"). Imperative gives commands ("Open the doors"). Subjunctive handles wishes, conditions contrary to fact, and demands ("I wish I were there"; "If she were taller, she would start"). An inappropriate mood shift jumps attitude mid-sentence: "If you finish your homework, please you will call me." Keep one mood: "If you finish your homework, call me."

The big rule for shifts: a shift is appropriate when it matches a real change in meaning or attitude — for example, instructions that switch from describing a fact to giving a command, or a report that moves to passive because the doer is unknown or unimportant. It is inappropriate when nothing in the meaning changed and the shift just sneaks up on the reader.

items.label: Cumulative

items.label: The subject acts
items.text: The subject of the sentence performs the action. The doer comes first and owns the verb.
items.example: Maria scored the winning goal.

items.label: Clear and direct
items.text: Active voice uses fewer words and tells the reader exactly who is responsible. It creates emphasis on the doer.
items.example: The committee approved the plan.

items.label: Stronger for most writing
items.text: When you want energy, accountability, or a clear story, reach for active voice first.
items.example: I made a mistake.

items.label: Not automatically wrong
items.text: Passive voice is a tool, not a bad habit. It is the right choice when the doer is unknown, when you want to be tactful, or when the receiver matters more.
items.example: My bike was stolen last night. (Doer unknown — nobody to name.)

items.label: Not the same as weak verbs
items.text: Passive is about who receives the action, not about word choice. 'The window was broken' is passive; 'The window shattered' is active.
items.example: Passive: The trophy was awarded to Nadia.

items.label: Not for hiding yourself carelessly
items.text: Sometimes writers use passive to dodge responsibility — 'Mistakes were made.' Choose passive for a reason, not to avoid one.
items.example: Tactful on purpose: The recipe was followed incorrectly.

blocks.purpose: States the anchor rule for mood — indicative states facts, imperative commands, conditional imagines with 'if/would', subjunctive expresses wishes or unreal situations — with prerequisites on verb forms.

data.anchor: Indicative states facts, imperative gives commands, conditional imagines with if and would, and subjunctive expresses wishes, demands, and unreal situations — usually with were instead of was.
prerequisites: Every sentence has a mood — the form of the verb that shows the speaker's attitude toward what they are saying.
Indicative: most sentences you write. 'The store closes at nine.' It states or asks about fact.
Imperative: the subject is usually an unstated 'you.' 'Close the door.' 'Please submit your essay by Friday.'
Conditional: an if/then situation that could happen. 'If it rains, we will move the picnic indoors.'
Subjunctive: contrary to fact or wished for. 'I wish I were taller.' 'If I were you, I would apologize.' The situation is not real, so English uses were, even with I, he, or she.

blocks.purpose: Compares voice/mood choices to a camera angle in a movie: the same scene told from different angles changes who the audience roots for, making the abstract grammar choice feel concrete.

analogies.because: Both choices do not change what happened — only who the camera is pointed at. Voice selects the subject that frames the sentence.
analogies.everydayScene: A director films the same soccer goal twice. Shot one: close on the striker's foot striking the ball. Shot two: close on the goalie's outstretched hands, just missing it. Identical event, completely different hero and villain.
analogies.mapsTo: Active voice points the camera at the doer: 'The striker scored.' Passive points it at the receiver: 'The goal was scored' — and the striker never appears on screen.

analogies.because: The same camera setting communicates a different attitude depending on where the scene could happen — real or imagined. Mood selects the verb form that tells the reader which world we are in.
analogies.everydayScene: Filmed as a documentary, a scene feels like fact: this happened. Filmed with a dreamy filter and 'what if' narration, the same scene feels imagined. A drill sergeant barking orders gives you a third feel entirely.
analogies.mapsTo: Indicative is documentary footage (fact). Imperative is the director shouting 'Action!' (command). Conditional is the 'what if' take ('If we had one more shot, we would win'). Subjunctive is the dream sequence ('I wish I were the hero').

data.bridgeStatement: Grammar is directing: same scene, different shot, different feeling.

data.context: Your school news article needs this sentence: the report's timing matters most, and nobody is sure which staff member actually submitted it.
data.question: Your English teacher marked every passive sentence in your essay and said to revise them. Given the assignment notes below, which sentence is actually the BEST choice?
data.recoveryTip: Before revising any passive sentence, ask: is the doer known, and is the doer the focus? If not, passive is doing its job.

trapReasons.1: It is active, but it names the principal as the doer — information the writer does not have, so it may be false.
trapReasons.2: Vague and weak; the passive original actually handles the unknown actor better.
trapReasons.3: Wordy and awkward — fixing voice is no excuse for a clunky sentence.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: The rule is not 'passive is wrong.' Passive is the right choice when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or when you want to emphasize the receiver. 'The principal submitted the report' sounds active and confident, but it invents a fact: it names the principal as the doer when nobody is sure.
data.correctReasoning: 'The report was submitted an hour before the deadline' keeps the emphasis on the report — the receiver, which is the real news — and it does not guess at an unknown doer. Choosing active here would add false information.

blocks.purpose: Anchors the four moods with a compact badge ('FACT, ORDER, IF, WISH') so indicative, imperative, conditional, and subjunctive are retrievable later.

expansions.phrase: Indicative — states fact or asks a question: 'The bus leaves at seven.'
Imperative — commands, subject is an unstated you: 'Take out the trash.'
Conditional — imagined but possible: 'If we hurried, we would catch it.'
Subjunctive — unreal or contrary to fact, uses were: 'I wish I were there.'

data.rationale: Run the four words in order before any revision pass: is this sentence stating fact, giving an order, imagining a possibility, or wishing for something unreal? The answer tells you which verb form to reach for.

blocks.purpose: Compact reference matrix of when to use each voice and mood, closing the lesson with a one-glance summary.

rows.detail: Best default for clarity and emphasis on the doer.
rows.value: Subject performs the action. Use it to be clear, direct, and to emphasize who did it.

rows.detail: Doer unknown, tact needed, or the receiver is the real news.
rows.value: Subject receives the action. Use it when the doer is unknown, when you need tact, or when the receiver deserves emphasis.
Choose voice for your purpose every time — never by habit, and never assume passive is wrong.
Statements of fact: 'She practices daily.'
Commands and instructions: 'Practice daily.'
Imagined if/then situations with would or could: 'If I practiced, I would improve.'

rows.detail: The situation is not real, so use were even with I, he, she, it.
rows.value: Wishes, demands, and contrary-to-fact statements: 'I wish I were,' 'If she were here, she would help.'
Keep one voice and one mood per sentence unless the change has a clear purpose; revise so the doer leads and the mood matches the meaning.
Two traps: calling all passive voice wrong, and using was where subjunctive were is required.

data.anchor: Dashes, colons, and semicolons are not decoration — each one tells the reader how long to pause and what to pay attention to.
prerequisites: A dash creates an abrupt, dramatic pause — like slamming on the brakes to make you notice what comes next.
A colon signals 'here it comes': it announces an explanation, a list, or a payoff after a complete sentence.
A semicolon joins two closely related complete sentences into one thought, tighter than a period but stronger than a comma.
A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences — that error is called a comma splice.
Reading a sentence aloud is the fastest way to feel which pause it needs.

analogies.everydayScene: Someone storms out and the door bangs shut — everything goes quiet for a beat, and you're startled into paying attention.

analogies.everydayScene: Rat-a-tat-tat... and then the big beat lands. The pause is a promise: the payoff is coming.

data.bridgeStatement: Punctuation is sound made visible — you can hear it before you can name it.

data.rule: Each punctuation mark creates a different length and character of pause, which changes a sentence's rhythm and emphasis.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side examples show what each mark adds versus what a plain comma or period gives, covering sentence_struct (fragments/run-ons) directly.

data.footnote: The fix: use a semicolon, a period, or a dash when two complete sentences meet. A comma can't hold them together.

items.label: Semicolon
items.text: A legal join between two closely related complete sentences.
items.example: The screen went black; the room stayed silent.

items.label: Colon
items.text: A complete sentence, then a payoff: an explanation or list.
items.example: I have one rule: never give up.

items.label: Dash
items.text: An abrupt pause for drama or emphasis.
items.example: The answer was obvious — to everyone but him.

items.label: Comma
items.text: A light pause inside a sentence, or items in a list.
items.example: I packed my bag, my coat, and my phone.

items.label: Comma splice
items.text: A comma can NOT join two complete sentences on its own — that creates a run-on error called a comma splice.
items.example: The screen went black, the room stayed silent.

items.label: Colon before 'such as'
items.text: A colon must follow a complete sentence — it can NOT sit before a list that starts with 'such as', 'including', or 'like'.
items.example: Wrong: I love sports such as: soccer and swimming.

items.label: Random swaps
items.text: You can't drop a semicolon in just anywhere; it needs two complete, closely related sentences on both sides.
items.example: Wrong: The dog; barked loudly.

items.label: A pause is not always a comma
items.text: Not every pause in speech needs a comma — many belong to dashes, colons, or nothing at all.
items.example: Wrong: The winner, was announced at noon.

blocks.purpose: Targets the #1 mistake — using a comma to splice two full sentences where a semicolon belongs — and reveals why intuition fails.

choices: The stage lights snapped on, the crowd went wild.
The stage lights snapped on; the crowd went wild.

data.commonErrorLabel: Using a comma between two complete sentences (comma splice)
data.context: The stage lights snapped on ... the crowd went wild. (Two complete sentences, closely related.)
data.correctReasoning: Both halves are complete sentences, and they're closely related. A semicolon is the correct tight join. A dash would add extra drama the sentence doesn't ask for, and a colon wouldn't fit the calm statement.
data.question: You want to keep these two related sentences joined smoothly, with no drama and no full stop. Which is correct?
data.recoveryTip: Ask yourself: are there complete sentences on both sides of the comma? If yes, swap the comma for a semicolon, a period, or a dash.

trapReasons.0: It sounds fine when read aloud — pauses often feel like commas — but two complete sentences can't legally be joined by a comma alone.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: When you read the comma version aloud, it sounds okay — speech pauses all the time between complete thoughts. But writing has stricter rules than speech: a comma alone can't hold two complete sentences together. That error is the comma splice, and it's the single most common punctuation mistake.

blocks.purpose: Sparks curiosity by presenting two plausible texts that differ only in punctuation — 'I'm fine...' vs 'I'm fine —' vs 'I'm fine,' — so learners feel how each mark changes tone before any rules appear.

data.context: Same two words. Different punctuation. Yet one sounds bored, one sounds tense, and one sounds like something got cut off mid-sentence. Before you learn the rules, trust that feeling — punctuation is tone.
data.footerNote: Three marks, three completely different moods. By the end of this lesson you will be able to pick the right one on purpose.

blocks.purpose: Teaches the core distinction side by side: comma = mild pause, dash = sharp break or emphasis, ellipsis = trailing off or omitted words, mapping all three coverage categories.

data.footnote: Mild pause = comma. Sharp break or emphasis = dash. Trailing off or left-out words = ellipsis.

items.label: Comma — mild pause
items.text: A soft beat inside a sentence: items in a series, an intro phrase, or a small extra detail tucked in.
items.example: I packed snacks, water, and a map. / After the bell rang, we left.

items.label: Dash — sharp break
items.text: A sudden stop, an interruption, or a dramatic emphasis. The dash slams the brakes.
items.example: I was about to tell you the secret— but never mind.

items.label: Ellipsis — trailing off or omitted words
items.text: Three dots show a voice fading out, a hesitation, or words you deliberately leave out of a quotation.
items.example: I thought you said you'd be here... / "I never said... that I was coming."

items.label: Comma is NOT a dramatic pause
items.text: If the break is sharp enough to interrupt someone or slam in emphasis, a comma is too weak.
items.example: Not: I saw the dog, the huge one, growling — that sharp side-comment deserves a dash.

items.label: Dash is NOT a soft connector
items.text: A dash creates a hard break. Ordinary list items and gentle details belong to the comma.
items.example: Not: apples — bananas — pears. / Right: apples, bananas, pears.

items.label: Ellipsis is NOT an all-purpose dot
items.text: Three dots do not simply make a sentence moodier, and they do not replace a period or question mark that the sentence needs.
items.example: Not: Why are you late... when a real question needs: Why are you late?

data.title: Comma vs. Dash vs. Ellipsis

blocks.purpose: Lays out the decision procedure: ask 'Is the pause mild, sharp, or trailing?' then choose comma, dash, or ellipsis, giving learners a reusable test for omissions and breaks.

steps.label: Feel the pause
steps.text: Find the spot where the sentence hesitates, breaks, or trails off.
steps.detail: Read it aloud and mark every place your voice naturally stops.

steps.label: Rate the pause
steps.text: Ask: is this pause mild, sharp, or trailing?
steps.detail: Mild = a soft beat. Sharp = an interruption or dramatic aside. Trailing = the voice fades or words are missing.

steps.label: Mild? Use a comma
steps.text: Commas handle series, intro phrases, and small side details.
steps.detail: Example: We grabbed our bags, checked the map, and started walking.

steps.label: Sharp? Use a dash
steps.text: Dashes handle interruptions, sudden turns, and strong emphasis.
steps.detail: Example: I was going to warn you— too late. He already saw us.

steps.label: Trailing or missing? Use an ellipsis
steps.text: Three dots show a fade-out or words you cut from a quotation.
steps.detail: If you cut words in the middle of a quoted sentence, put three dots where the words used to be.

steps.label: Check the end of the sentence
steps.text: A complete sentence still needs its period or question mark — an ellipsis does not replace them.
steps.detail: If an ellipsis sits at the very end of a finished sentence, add a fourth dot: the period.

blocks.purpose: Clarifies underlined technical terms — omission, parenthetical, ellipsis, dash, hyphen — so learners don't confuse a dash with a hyphen or misuse 'omission.'

data.footer: Know the names and you will never grab a hyphen when you need a dash.
data.heading: The vocabulary of pauses
data.sentence: When you {omission} part of a quotation, you use an {ellipsis}. Inside a sentence, a {parenthetical} is a side comment set off by a {dash} — and a dash is not the same key as the little {hyphen} on your keyboard.

terms.definition: Words or letters deliberately left out, usually to shorten a quotation or to imply something unsaid.
terms.hint: Example: "I was going to the store..." leaves out the rest of the sentence.
terms.label: omission

terms.definition: A set of three dots (...) showing a hesitation, a trailing-off voice, or omitted words in a quotation.
terms.hint: Not one dot, not six — exactly three (plus a fourth at the end of a finished sentence).
terms.label: ellipsis

terms.definition: Extra information dropped into a sentence that could be removed and the sentence would still make sense.
terms.hint: Example: My brother — the one with the scooter — fixed it.
terms.label: parenthetical

terms.definition: A long mark (—) used for a sharp break, interruption, or emphasis inside a sentence.
terms.hint: On most keyboards, type two hyphens or use the em dash symbol.
terms.label: dash

terms.definition: A short mark (-) that joins words together, like in ice-cream or check-in.
terms.hint: A hyphen joins; a dash breaks.
terms.label: hyphen

blocks.purpose: Warns against the #1 errors: using ellipsis to dodge a period, confusing dash with hyphen, and over-punctuating — the non-examples and exceptions for all three marks.

cautions.detail: An ellipsis shows missing or fading words. It does not stand in for the end punctuation a real sentence needs.
cautions.title: Do NOT use an ellipsis instead of a period or question mark

cautions.detail: A dash (—) is long and breaks a sentence apart. A hyphen (-) is short and glues words together.
cautions.exampleNote: Two hyphens typed together (-- ) are usually accepted as a dash, but a single short hyphen is never a dash.
cautions.title: A dash is NOT a hyphen
cautions.wrongExample: I can't believe- wait, is that him?
cautions.rightExample: I can't believe— wait, is that him?

cautions.detail: If the omission happens where a full sentence ends, use three dots plus the period — four dots total.
cautions.title: Four dots when the omission ends a full sentence
cautions.wrongExample: "I'll be there at six... See you."
cautions.rightExample: "I'll be there at six.... See you."

cautions.detail: One pause point gets one mark. Piling on commas, dashes, and dots makes writing feel twitchy and confusing.
cautions.rightExample: Honestly, we were all exhausted by Friday.
cautions.title: Do NOT over-punctuate
cautions.wrongExample: Honestly —, we were all... exhausted... by Friday —

data.flagIntro: The three marks are easy to mix up, and each one has a temptation you should refuse.
data.footerNote: When in doubt, read it aloud: if the sentence ends cleanly, end punctuation wins.

blocks.purpose: Defines what a style guide is with a bolded anchor sentence and prerequisite bullets, covering the core idea that style guides settle disputed rules.

data.anchor: A style guide is a reference book of agreed-upon choices that settles disputed usage questions — it tells writers which option to follow, even when the rules of English allow more than one.
prerequisites: Grammar gives you the hard rules: a sentence needs a subject and a verb, and words must fit together. Those are not debatable.
Usage is different: it covers choices like which word to pick or where to put a comma, where several options are grammatically possible.
Some word pairs get mixed up so often (affect and effect) that editors argue about them too — which makes them perfect examples of usage questions.
A fragment is an incomplete sentence and a run-on jams sentences together; both are errors, not style choices — knowing the difference matters later in this lesson.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side comparison of two real style guides (e.g., AP vs. Chicago) showing how they disagree on a specific disputed rule like the Oxford comma.

data.footnote: A style guide settles disputed usage by declaring a house choice — it does not discover the one true answer.

items.label: A set of choices
items.text: A decision manual for questions where two reasonable answers exist. It picks one so everyone in a newsroom, publishing house, or school writes the same way.
items.example: Chicago says: use the Oxford comma. AP says: leave it out.

items.label: Consistency
items.text: The main goal is not perfection — it is sameness. Readers should never notice the style flipping mid-article.

items.label: Changeable
items.text: Guides get revised every few years. When real-world usage shifts, the guide updates to match it.

rightColumn.heading: What a style guide is NOT

items.label: Not the grammar police
items.text: A style guide does not override hard grammar rules. No guide allows fragments or run-ons in formal writing.
items.example: "She went to the store. Because she was hungry." stays an error under every guide.

items.label: Not universal law
items.text: Two guides can give opposite answers to the same question, and both are correct within their own system. There is no Supreme Court of English.

items.label: Not eternal truth
items.text: A rule inside a guide can be dropped in the next edition. The guide follows usage; it does not command it.

blocks.purpose: Tells the short story of a real usage debate (e.g., split infinitives or singular 'they') that caused style guides to change, showing rules evolve over time.

beforeAfter.after: Editors slowly gave up. Chicago dropped its ban in 2014, and most guides now accept split infinitives when splitting sounds better. Usage had already changed — the rules followed.
beforeAfter.before: Style guides and teachers banned split infinitives for over a century. Careful writers contorted sentences to keep "to" and its verb together, often making them clunkier.

data.crisis: English grammar handbooks copied Latin patterns, and in Latin an infinitive is one word that cannot be split. So 19th-century editors declared that English infinitives must never be split either — a rule with no real basis in how English works.
story: The rule made famous by Star Trek's "to boldly go" — with "boldly" wedged inside the infinitive "to go" — had been attacked since the 1800s. Grammar writers insisted the adverb belonged before the whole phrase: "boldly to go."

But no English speaker actually talked that way. Famous writers kept splitting infinitives on purpose because the split version often sounds stronger and clearer. The ban survived mostly on habit and snobbery.
data.takeaway: When everyday usage and a rule collide for long enough, usage usually wins — style guides update, and yesterday's "error" becomes a choice.

cards.answer: Active voice: the subject does the action, like 'The dog chased the ball.' It sounds clear and energetic. Passive voice: the subject receives the action, like 'The ball was chased by the dog.' Writers pick passive on purpose when the doer is unknown or the receiver matters.

cards.answer: Dash: emphasis or an abrupt break, and it sets off extra info louder than parentheses. Colon: introduces a list or explanation, and a complete sentence must come before it. Semicolon: joins two closely related complete sentences, often with transition words like 'however.'

data.anchor: Active voice puts the subject in charge: it does the action. Passive voice puts the subject on the receiving end: the action is done to it. Both are correct — the writer picks based on what deserves the spotlight.
prerequisites: Formation: active = subject + verb + object ('Maya scored the goal'). Passive = form of 'be' + past participle ('The goal was scored by Maya').
Active creates clarity and energy: shorter, more direct, and it keeps the doer visible. Default to it in most writing.
Passive is deliberate and correct when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or when the receiver matters more: 'My bike was stolen last night.'
Neither voice is an error. Flipping between them without a reason is the real problem — that is an unintentional shift.

data.title: Dash, Colon, or Semicolon?

blocks.purpose: Targets the #1 punctuation mistake: using a semicolon where a colon is needed because a complete sentence must precede a colon.

choices: The tournament has one strict rule; no trash talking allowed.
The tournament has one strict rule, no trash talking allowed.
The tournament has one strict rule: no trash talking allowed.
The tournament has one strict rule - no trash talking allowed.
data.commonErrorLabel: Semicolon where a colon is needed
data.context: "The tournament has one strict rule; no trash talking allowed."
data.correctReasoning: The sentence introduces an explanation of the rule, so it needs a colon. 'The tournament has one strict rule' is a complete sentence on its own, which is exactly the requirement a colon has before it. The colon signals 'here it comes' — and the rule follows.
data.question: Which revision uses punctuation correctly?
data.recoveryTip: Before any punctuation, ask: am I introducing something (colon) or joining two full sentences (semicolon)? If a list or explanation follows, reach for the colon.

trapReasons.0: The semicolon looks formal and 'fancy', so it feels right even though nothing is being joined.
trapReasons.1: The comma is the everyday default, but here it creates a comma splice — two independent ideas glued with too weak a mark.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: The semicolon feels sophisticated, so it seems like the 'smart' choice. But a semicolon's only job is to join two closely related complete sentences. Here, 'no trash talking allowed' is not a complete sentence, so there is nothing to join — the sentence is introducing an explanation instead.

blocks.purpose: Compare raw punctuated text vs a polished version using ellipses for trailing/hesitation, dashes for abrupt breaks, and commas for softer pauses, covering omitted words.

after.body: I started to say something — something I'd rehearsed all week — but the words just trailed off... "I, um, wanted to say, thanks for coming." She smiled, waited, and let the silence do the rest.
after.caption: Ellipsis for the trail-off, dashes for the interruption, commas for the soft beats.
after.label: After
points: Ellipsis shows her words trailing off into hesitation
Dashes mark the interrupted thought with force
Commas give the dialogue a nervous, halting rhythm
after.title: Hesitation on the Page

before.body: I started to say something. Something I'd rehearsed all week. But the words just stopped. I wanted to say. Thanks for coming. She smiled and let the silence do the rest.
before.caption: Every break becomes a full stop, so nothing feels hesitant or interrupted.
before.label: Before
points: Full stops make a hesitant moment sound choppy and robotic
The interrupted thought ('Something I'd rehearsed all week') reads as a fragment with no signal of why it broke
No pause marks, so the reader can't hear the character stalling
before.title: Flat Full Stops

data.conceptSubtitle: Same story, different marks — listen to how the pauses change the voice.

data.summaryBody: A rule is settled when every authority agrees. When authorities disagree, a style guide decides — and you follow the guide your audience expects, consistently.

blocks.purpose: Learner fills blanks in a short paragraph choosing active/passive and mood forms, plus the right pause punctuation, applying all four lessons in one passage.

acceptedAnswers: the goal was scored by the rookie in overtime
the goal was scored in overtime by the rookie
data.context: Rewrite this in passive voice, keeping the receiver 'the goal' as the subject: The rookie scored the goal in overtime. ______
data.explanation: Passive voice moves the receiver to the subject position: form of 'be' plus a past participle. Here 'the goal' receives the action, so it becomes the subject: 'The goal was scored by the rookie in overtime.' Notice the doer does not disappear — it slides into a 'by' phrase.
data.errorMessage: Not quite. Check that 'the goal' is the subject and that you used a form of 'be' plus a past participle (was scored).
data.prompt: Turn the active sentence into passive voice.
data.successMessage: Exactly — the receiver takes the spotlight.

blocks.purpose: Compact key-value matrix summarizing every rule from all four lessons as the final anchor for later topics on diction and tone.

rows.value: Subject does the action: 'Maya scored.' Clear and energetic — your default.
Form of 'be' + past participle: 'The goal was scored by Maya.' Deliberate choice when the doer is unknown or the receiver matters.
If + present, will + verb: 'If it rains, we will stay.' A real, possible condition.
Wishes, hypotheticals, demands: 'If I were you' and 'She insists that he be on time.' Bare base verb is the tell.
Shifts are author choices for emphasis and tone — only unintentional, confusing shifts are problems.
Emphasis or an abrupt break; sets off extra info louder than parentheses: 'My brother — the quiet one — won.'
Introduces a list or explanation; a complete sentence must come first: 'She had one rule: never give up.'
Joins two closely related complete sentences, with or without 'however', 'therefore': 'I practiced daily; however, I still struggled.'
If the second part is not a complete sentence, you are introducing something — use a colon, not a semicolon.
Ellipsis trails off or omits words... dash breaks suddenly — commas pause softly.
Split infinitives, singular 'they', serial commas: authorities disagree, so style guides settle it — follow yours consistently.
Diction and precision, then tone control — voice and mood will be your toolkit.

plans.approach: A typical 14-year-old learns diction best by seeing the same idea rewritten at different word "sizes" and by fixing imprecise sentences themselves, so the sequence moves from concrete word swaps to tone/audience control and common confusions. Practice follows each teach block, and a compact cheat sheet plus a takeaway badge consolidate the rules for retention.
coverage: Diction defined: choosing the exact word for meaning, tone, and audience
Denotation vs connotation: dictionary meaning vs feelings a word carries
Precision beats vagueness: replacing generic words (good, thing, got) with specific ones
Fancy is not better: when a simpler word is the more precise choice
Tone: a word's emotional coloring changes the sentence's attitude
Audience and register: formal vs informal word choice for the reader and situation
Commonly confused words that change meaning (affect/effect, fewer/less, its/it's)
Editing for precision: finding and fixing weak or wrong-toned words in a draft

blocks.purpose: Opens with a split-card dilemma: should a student email a teacher 'The project is finished' or 'I have completed the project' — same meaning, different effect — to activate prior knowledge of voice and mood from previous topics.

data.prompt: Your essay is due in ten minutes. Which email do you send your teacher?
data.context: Both sentences say the same thing. But they do not feel the same. Last unit you learned how voice and mood change a reader's reaction — now watch how a single word choice does the same job.

leftChoice.label: OPTION A
leftChoice.title: The project is finished.
leftChoice.body: Short, blunt, and a little flat. It sounds like a text to a friend, not an update to a teacher.

rightChoice.label: OPTION B
rightChoice.title: I have completed the project.
rightChoice.body: Same message, same length almost, but it sounds responsible and complete. Nothing was added — only the words were chosen more carefully.

data.footerNote: Neither sentence is grammatically wrong. So what makes one the better choice? That question is what this lesson answers.

blocks.purpose: Anchor definition of diction: choosing the exact word for meaning, tone, and audience, with prerequisite bullets (denotation vs connotation, word strength, reader awareness).

data.anchor: Diction is the craft of choosing the exact word that fits your meaning, your tone, and your audience — not just any word that is close enough.
prerequisites: Denotation vs connotation: a word's denotation is its dictionary definition; its connotation is the feeling or attitude that hangs around it (cheap vs thrifty).
Word strength: some words are vague catch-alls (good, thing, got) while others carry exact, specific meaning (excellent, backpack, inherited).
Reader awareness: you already choose different words when texting a friend than when emailing a principal — that instinct is the starting point for controlling it on purpose.

blocks.purpose: Shows a vague paragraph ('got, stuff, did things') beside a precise rewrite, proving that replacing generic words with specific ones sharpens meaning without lengthening.

data.conceptSubtitle: Same event, same length — only the word choices changed.
data.prompt: Slide the divider to compare. Look for the vague words: got, stuff, did things.

before.label: Before
before.title: The Vague Draft
before.body: Yesterday I got some stuff at the store and then I did things at home, and it was good because I got a lot done before I went to bed.
points: Got appears three times — it could mean bought, received, found, or reached.
Stuff and things name nothing you can picture.
Good tells us a feeling, not a fact.
The reader finishes the paragraph knowing almost nothing.
before.caption: Vague words make the reader guess.

after.label: After
after.title: The Precise Rewrite
after.body: Yesterday I bought sketch pencils at the art store, then finished my history outline at the kitchen table, and I got to bed early feeling accomplished.
points: Bought says exactly how the items were obtained.
Sketch pencils and history outline give the reader a picture.
Accomplished names the feeling with evidence behind it.
Notice: the rewrite is not longer than the draft.
after.caption: Exact words sharpen meaning without adding bulk.

data.footerNote: Precision beats vagueness. You rarely need more words — you need better ones.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side comparison of denotation vs connotation and formal vs informal diction, so learners see one word can be correct and still the wrong choice.

data.title: Correct vs. Right: Denotation, Connotation, and Register
data.subtitle: A word can be perfectly correct and still be the wrong choice for the sentence.

items.label: Denotation first
items.text: Check the literal meaning: does the word actually name what you mean?
items.example: A skillet denotes a frying pan — the dictionary agrees either way.

items.label: Connotation second
items.text: Then check the feeling: does the word carry the attitude you want?
items.example: Thrifty and stingy both denote spending little, but thrifty praises and stingy blames.

items.label: Register match
items.text: Match the formality of your words to your audience and situation.
items.example: Email a teacher: I have completed the assignment. Text a friend: done with it.

items.label: Not fancy words
items.text: A thesaurus swap is not automatically an upgrade. Big words that don't fit break tone and confuse readers.
items.example: I utilized the commode to facilitate my hygiene routine. (Just say: I used the sink to wash up.)

items.label: Not emotion-free
items.text: Every content word has a color. Ignore it and your sentence says more — or less — than you meant.
items.example: The puppy was inexpensive vs. the puppy was cheap: same price, different respect.

items.label: Not one-size-fits-all
items.text: There is no single best word. The exact word depends on who is reading and why.
items.example: Passed away, died, and lost all denote the same event — for a condolence card, choose the gentlest one.

data.footnote: The test is never is this word fancy? It is: does this word mean, feel, and fit exactly right?

blocks.purpose: First retrieval: pick the word whose connotation fits a given audience and tone (e.g., 'thrifty' vs 'stingy' for a recommendation letter).

data.prompt: You are writing the character reference paragraph of a recommendation letter for a classmate. Which word best fits the audience and the positive tone you need?
data.passage: Maria is very ______ with money — she compared prices, used a coupon, and still got everything on the list for the bake sale.

options.text: stingy
thrifty
cheap
miserly

feedback.correct: Thrifty means careful with money and carries a compliment — exactly what a recommendation letter needs.
feedback.incorrect: All four words denote the same behavior, but three of them carry an insult. In a letter that praises Maria, an insult is the wrong connotation.

byOption.a: Stingy blames the person for being unwilling to share — the opposite of a compliment.
byOption.c: Cheap suggests poor quality or stinginess; it would sink a recommendation letter.
byOption.d: Miserly is correct in denotation but sounds like an accusation, and it is overly formal for a school letter.

blocks.purpose: Targets the #1 mistake: choosing big or 'fancy' words instead of exact ones, showing why thesaurus swaps often break tone or meaning.

data.question: Your history essay needs one revision of this sentence: After the war, the economy got really bad. Which revision is the most precise AND fits a formal essay?
data.context: Working draft sentence: After the war, the economy got really bad.
choices: After the war, the economy was super terrible.
After the war, the economy collapsed into a catastrophic maelstrom of ruin.
After the war, unemployment doubled and prices rose sharply.
After the war, the economy was not so good.
data.commonErrorLabel: Choosing big or dramatic words over exact ones

trapReasons.0: Super terrible is stronger than bad, but it is still vague and too casual for an essay.
trapReasons.1: This sounds impressive, but a maelstrom of ruin is a swirl of water — it does not denote anything an economy does.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: The instinct is that upgrading to bigger, more dramatic words must be an improvement. But precision is about matching meaning, not raising volume. Super terrible is vaguer than the original, and catastrophic maelstrom of ruin is dramatic theater that does not literally describe an economy — a thesaurus swap gone wrong.
data.correctReasoning: Unemployment doubled and prices rose sharply replaces the vague phrase got really bad with two specific, checkable facts. Every word denotes something exact, the register fits a formal essay, and no fancy vocabulary is needed.
data.recoveryTip: After every word swap, ask: does the new word name something a reader could picture or check? If not, it is decoration, not precision.

blocks.purpose: A sentence with underlined terms (denotation, connotation, register, euphemism) revealing plain-English definitions so vocabulary-in-context skill is practised in place.

data.heading: Decode the terms as you read
data.sentence: When editors evaluate a writer's {denotation} problems, they look past the dictionary definition to the {connotation} a word carries, then judge whether the word suits the {register} of the piece — and if a blunt truth would sound cruel, a careful writer may soften it with a {euphemism}.

terms.label: denotation
terms.definition: The literal, dictionary meaning of a word — the thing it names no matter who says it.
terms.hint: Snake denotes a legless reptile; that is the denotation.

terms.label: connotation
terms.definition: The feelings and attitudes a word carries beyond its literal meaning.
terms.hint: Sly carries a sneaky feeling even when you call a person a snake as a joke.

terms.label: register
terms.definition: The level of formality in word choice, matched to the audience and situation.
terms.hint: Texting BRB and writing 'I will return shortly' are different registers.

terms.label: euphemism
terms.definition: A mild or pleasant word used in place of a blunt or harsh one.
terms.hint: Saying passed away instead of died is a euphemism.

data.footer: Tap each underlined term. Being able to define these in your own words is half of vocabulary in context.

data.title: Find the Weak Words
data.instructions: Tap every word that is too vague or wrongly toned for this formal book-report sentence. There are four.
data.paragraph: The book was really good and the main character got really upset about a bunch of stuff that happened at her new school.

tokens.explanation: Really is an empty intensifier — it adds no meaning in formal writing.
Good is a vague catch-all: good how? Funny? Suspenseful? Name the quality.
Got is imprecise — became upset or grew furious says exactly what happened.
This second really is another empty intensifier.

data.successMessage: All four found. A precise rewrite: The novel was suspenseful, and the main character became furious about the bullying she faced at her new school.
data.incompleteMessage: Some weak words are still hiding. Look for intensifiers, catch-alls like good, and vague verbs like got.

checks.prompt: Your teacher praises Maya in a note home: Maya is very ______ about her homework — she checks every answer twice before turning it in. Which word fits the blank and carries the right connotation?
checks.answer: Diligent
checks.rationale: All four words could loosely describe checking work twice, but only diligent carries the approving connotation the note needs; lazy, slow, and picky all blame her.
checks.hint: Both lazy and slow describe low effort. The blank praises Maya — pick the praise word.
choices: Lazy
Diligent
Slow
Picky
checks.focus: Choose the word with the right connotation for the context

checks.prompt: In the lesson, connotation is defined as which of the following?
checks.answer: The feelings a word carries beyond its literal meaning
checks.rationale: Connotation is the emotional coloring attached to a word; the literal meaning is denotation, the formality level is register, and the softened word is a euphemism.
checks.hint: Denotation is the dictionary meaning — connotation is what a word suggests beyond that.
choices: The literal dictionary meaning of a word
The feelings a word carries beyond its literal meaning
The level of formality matched to the audience
A mild word used in place of a harsh one

checks.answer: fewer
checks.rationale: Players are countable items, so the rule fewer for countable nouns decides the answer; less is reserved for amounts you cannot count.
checks.hint: Count the players — you can count them one by one.
choices: less
fewer
fewer or less
less than

checks.prompt: Which option is a complete, precise sentence rather than a fragment? A: Because the stadium lights flickered during the storm. B: The stadium lights flickered during the storm, and the announcer paused the broadcast. C: Flickering wildly, the announcer paused the broadcast during the storm. D: The stadium lights, flickering during the storm last Tuesday night.
checks.answer: B
checks.rationale: Only B has a full subject and verb in each clause and names exact actions; A is a subordinate fragment, C dangles its modifier so the wrong thing flickers, and D is a subject with no main verb.
checks.hint: A fragment is missing its subject or its verb. Check that each option has both and states something exact.
choices: A
B
C
D
checks.focus: Choose the sentence that is a complete, precise statement rather than a fragment

checks.answer: B

coverage: A complete sentence needs a subject, a finite verb, and a complete thought
A fragment is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought

A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma

Fix a run-on with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS)

options.text: Complete — it has a subject (the bells) and a verb (rang), so it is a full sentence.
options.whyNot: It does have those parts, but the word Although turns the whole thing into a dependent clause. A dependent clause leaning on nothing is still a fragment.

options.text: Fragment — Although makes this a dependent clause, so the thought is incomplete on its own.
options.whyNot: Correct. The subordinating word stops the clause from standing alone; it needs an independent clause to attach to.

options.text: Fixable with just a comma — write: Although the bells rang, and leave it there.
options.whyNot: A comma cannot finish a dependent clause. You must add an independent clause, not just punctuation.

data.decisionPrompt: Rewrite the broken sentence so it is fully correct. You may add punctuation, a joining word (FANBOYS), or a subordinating word — and you may split it into more than one sentence if that is cleanest.

misconception.detail: Fixing the fragment or the splice with only a comma does not work. A comma alone cannot join independent clauses (that creates a splice), and no punctuation can complete a dependent clause on its own. Use a period, semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS for the clauses, and attach the dependent clause to a complete sentence.

rule.name: The Repair Rules
rule.statement: A complete sentence needs a subject, a finite verb, and a complete thought. Fix a fused run-on with a period, a semicolon, a comma + FANBOYS, or a subordinating word. Never join two independent clauses with only a comma.

data.scenarioBody: A student submitted this sentence to the school paper: Although the stage was crowded the soloist found her spotlight, she sang the final verse the audience fell silent. Two problems are hiding in it: a fused run-on, and a subordinate clause left standing alone. Your job is to rebuild the sentence so it is fully correct — and say which repair rules you used.

targetAnswer.decision: Although the stage was crowded, the soloist found her spotlight. She sang the final verse, and the audience fell silent. (Also correct: use a semicolon — 'She sang the final verse; the audience fell silent.')
targetAnswer.rationale: The original hides three problems. 'Although the stage was crowded' is a subordinate-clause fragment standing alone, so it must be attached to a complete sentence with a comma after 'crowded.' 'The soloist found her spotlight, she sang the final verse' is a comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses. Fix it by starting a new sentence with a period, or keep it in one sentence with a semicolon or a comma + FANBOYS. Finally, 'the final verse the audience fell silent' is a fused run-on with no punctuation at all, so it needs a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction (here 'and' works well).

checks.prompt: What exactly makes a group of words a fragment?
checks.answer: A fragment is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.
checks.rationale: The deciding step: a complete sentence needs a subject, a finite verb, and a complete thought, so a fragment is defined by missing one of those three — not by length or its first word.
checks.hint: Recall the three requirements of a complete sentence — a fragment is missing one of them.
choices: A fragment is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.
A fragment is a very short sentence with only a few words.
A fragment is any sentence that starts with a subordinating word.
A fragment is a sentence with more than one subject.
checks.focus: Definitions of complete sentence, fragment, run-on, comma splice

checks.prompt: Into the box. In the final minute, kicked the ball over the fence.
checks.answer: Fragment — there is no subject: who was kicking?
checks.rationale: Kicked is a finite verb and the thought is complete, but there is no subject telling us who kicked — so it fails one of the three requirements and is a fragment.
checks.hint: Check the three requirements one at a time. Kicked is a verb — but whose foot did the kicking?
choices: Fragment — there is no subject: who was kicking?
Complete — the ball receives the action of kicked.
Complete — kicked is a finite verb, so it counts.
Fragment — a sentence cannot start with the word In.
checks.focus: Identifying a fragment missing a subject

checks.prompt: Is this a complete sentence or a fragment? Answer with one word. When the lights went out during the play.
checks.answer: fragment
checks.rationale: The subordinating word When makes the clause dependent, and a dependent clause with nothing attached lacks a complete thought — so it is a fragment.
checks.hint: Because is a subordinating word. Can a clause it starts with stand alone?
checks.focus: Subordinate-clause fragment vs complete sentence

checks.prompt: The concert ended the crowd sang the last chorus together. What is the error?
checks.answer: Run-on — the second clause is fused on with no punctuation at all.
checks.rationale: The crowd sang... is an independent clause attached with no punctuation whatsoever between the clauses — that fusion is the definition of a run-on, distinct from a comma splice.
checks.hint: Look closely at what sits between the two clauses. Is there anything there?
choices: Run-on — the second clause is fused on with no punctuation at all.
Comma splice — a comma sits between the two clauses.
Complete — the semicolon joins the two clauses correctly.
Fragment — the second part has no subject.
checks.focus: Spotting a run-on in running text

checks.prompt: The museum closed at six, we had forty minutes left. One word of punctuation fixes this while keeping both clauses closely linked. Which single punctuation mark is the best fix here? (One word.)
checks.answer: semicolon
checks.rationale: The clauses are closely related and the sentence needs no added conjunction, so the semicolon is the best single-mark fix; a comma alone would still be a splice.
checks.hint: The two clauses are closely related, and you want the punctuation alone to do the joining — no extra word needed.
checks.focus: Choosing the correct fix (semicolon vs comma + FANBOYS)

checks.prompt: Fix this broken sentence in full: Because the rehearsal ran late. The stage crew worked until midnight. (Write the whole corrected sentence, joining it into one.)
checks.answer: Because the rehearsal ran late, the stage crew worked until midnight.
checks.rationale: Because... is a subordinate-clause fragment; attaching it to the independent clause with a comma makes one correct complex sentence.
accepts: Because the rehearsal ran late, the stage crew worked until midnight.
because the rehearsal ran late, the stage crew worked until midnight
checks.hint: Make the first clause dependent with a subordinating word so it attaches to the complete second clause.

options.text: Because the bus was late.
options.whyNot: Tempting: it has a subject (bus) and a verb (was late). But it starts with because, so it is a subordinate clause — it leaves the thought hanging. It needs to attach to a main clause.

options.text: The bus was late.
options.whyNot: It survives: it has a subject (bus), a finite verb (was), and a complete thought. No subordinating word, so nothing is left hanging.

options.text: The bus was late we walked home.
options.whyNot: Tempting: it looks like two solid sentences glued together. But two independent clauses with no punctuation is a run-on, not a fragment.

options.text: The bus was late, we walked home.
options.whyNot: Tempting: the comma makes it look tidy. But a comma between two independent clauses is a comma splice — still a run-on.

data.scenarioBody: You are the student editor of the Science Club newsletter. A volunteer wrote this line for the front page: "The annual bake sale is this Saturday we need volunteers for two shifts." Your advisor says it reads fine out loud but breaks a grammar rule on paper, and the print deadline is Friday. The sentence must stay under 30 words and keep both facts.

targetAnswer.decision: The annual bake sale is this Saturday, so we need volunteers for two shifts. (Also correct: "The annual bake sale is this Saturday; we need volunteers for two shifts." or "The annual bake sale is this Saturday. We need volunteers for two shifts.")
targetAnswer.rationale: The original line is a fused run-on: two independent clauses joined with no punctuation. I joined them with a comma plus the FANBOYS conjunction so, which is one of the four approved repairs.

blocks.purpose: Resist tempting wrong answers about why 'Because I said so.' is a fragment and why two independent clauses need more than a comma.

options.text: It is a fragment because it is too short to be a real sentence.
options.whyNot: Tempting, but wrong. Length has nothing to do with it. Two words ('Birds sing.') form a complete sentence. 'Because I said so.' is a fragment because of what it is missing, not how long it is.

options.text: It is a fragment because it does not end with a period in the right place.
options.whyNot: Tempting, but wrong. The punctuation at the end is fine. The problem lives inside the sentence, not at its edge.

options.text: It is a fragment because 'said so' is not a real verb phrase.
options.whyNot: Tempting, but wrong. 'Said' is a perfectly good finite verb with the subject 'I'. The verb is not the problem.

options.text: It is a fragment because the subordinating word 'because' turns the whole thing into a dependent clause that leaves a thought unfinished.
options.whyNot: This survives scrutiny. A subordinating word promises an answer ('because' what?) and the clause alone never delivers it. 'Because I said so.' has a subject and a verb, but no complete thought — that is exactly the subordinate-clause fragment.

data.prompt: A classmate says: 'Because I said so.' is a complete sentence — it has a subject (I) and a verb (said). Why is that classmate wrong?

rule.name: Pattern matches purpose
rule.statement: Choose a sentence pattern deliberately: use a periodic sentence to build suspense, a cumulative sentence to deliver the point fast and then pile up detail, and a balanced sentence to create symmetry (or antithesis for contrast). Every complete sentence still needs a subject, a finite verb, and a complete thought, and no two independent clauses can be joined by only a comma.

data.scenarioBody: The librarian has asked you to write the announcement that will go up in the hallway and out to families by email. It must be memorable, because last year only nine people signed up. The fun run starts at 9:00 a.m. at the boathouse on Saturday, June 14, and the money raised buys new books for the town library. Sign-ups close Thursday. You have a word budget of three sentences — so every sentence has to do real work.
data.scenarioTitle: One Poster, Three Sentences: The Riverside Fun Run

targetAnswer.decision: Sample answer: If you can walk, jog, or sprint three flat kilometers along the river, you should sign up by Thursday. (periodic) The fun run starts at 9:00 a.m. at the boathouse on Saturday, June 14, with every dollar buying new books for the town library. (cumulative) Walkers raise hope, runners raise money, and the library raises everyone. (balanced, with antithesis)
targetAnswer.rationale: The periodic sentence saves the main clause (sign up by Thursday) for the end, so the reader arrives at the deadline with the punch — suspense matching the purpose of getting sign-ups. The cumulative sentence leads with the main clause (the fun run starts) and piles on detail (time, place, date, cause) so families get the facts fast and richly. The balanced sentence sets parallel contrasting parts (walkers / runners / the library) in similar structure, creating symmetry with antithesis so the closing line is quotable and sticks in the memory.

checks.prompt: In your own words, define a periodic sentence, a cumulative sentence, and a balanced sentence. (One short line each.)
checks.answer: A periodic sentence saves the main clause for the end to build suspense and deliver a punch. A cumulative sentence starts with the main clause and then piles up detail. A balanced sentence has two or more parallel parts of similar length and structure.
checks.rationale: The deciding step is the position of the main clause: periodic saves it for the end, cumulative opens with it, and balanced uses two parallel parts of similar length and structure.
accepts: periodic saves the main clause for the end; cumulative starts with it and adds detail; balanced has parallel similar parts
periodic: main clause last; cumulative: main clause first then detail; balanced: two parallel parts of similar length and structure
checks.hint: The key difference between periodic and cumulative is where the main clause sits.

checks.prompt:
Which of these is a complete sentence?
A. Running down the hall with my backpack half open.
B. She sprinted down the hall with her backpack half open.
checks.answer: B only; A is a fragment
checks.rationale: A has no finite verb (running is not finite) and no subject, so it is a fragment; B has a subject (she), a finite verb (sprinted), and a complete thought.
checks.hint: Look for the finite verb, not just for action-sounding words.
choices: Both are complete sentences
A only; B is a fragment
B only; A is a fragment
Neither is a complete sentence

checks.prompt: My phone battery died, I borrowed a charger. The comma here is a comma splice. Which fix is correct?
checks.answer: Replace the comma with a semicolon: My phone battery died; I borrowed a charger
checks.rationale: The deciding rule: two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone. A semicolon is one of the approved fixes; another comma is not.
checks.hint: A comma alone is exactly the thing that makes this a comma splice.
choices: Add a comma before 'I' to make the pause clearer
Replace the comma with a semicolon: My phone battery died; I borrowed a charger
Change the comma to a period and delete 'I borrowed a charger'
Leave it alone; a comma is all two clauses need
checks.focus: Name the correct fix (semicolon, FANBOYS, period) for a given run-on

checks.prompt: Why can a subordinate clause such as 'When the game finally started' not stand alone as a sentence? Answer in a short phrase.
checks.answer: The subordinating word makes the clause dependent: it cannot stand alone and finish the thought
checks.rationale: The subordinating word signals that the clause depends on another clause to complete the thought; without one, it is a subordinate-clause fragment even though it has a subject and a verb.
accepts: because the subordinating word makes it dependent, so it has no complete thought
it depends on another clause to finish the thought
checks.hint: The subordinating word creates a promise the clause cannot keep by itself.
checks.focus: Explain why a subordinate clause cannot stand alone

checks.prompt: We came to cheer, we stayed to sweat. Which pattern and effect does this show?
checks.answer: Balanced — two similar structures create symmetry
checks.rationale: Two parallel clauses of similar length and structure create the symmetry of a balanced sentence; nothing is contrasted or saved for last.
checks.hint: Look at the shape: two parts mirroring each other, not one clause plus extras.
choices: Periodic — it saves the punch for the end
Cumulative — the detail piles up after the main clause
Balanced — two similar structures create symmetry
Antithesis — it contrasts two opposite ideas
checks.focus: Match each sentence pattern to its rhetorical effect

checks.prompt: Combine these into one correct sentence: the fragment 'Although the storm rolled in' and the independent clause 'the match went on.'
checks.answer: Although the storm rolled in, the match went on.
checks.rationale: The fragment is a dependent clause, so it becomes correct the moment it is attached to an independent clause that supplies the complete thought.
accepts: Though the storm rolled in, the match went on.
The match went on even though the storm rolled in.
Although the storm rolled in, the match went on.
