blocks.purpose: Learner picks which statement about word order and emphasis is true, resisting tempting flawed options (e.g., 'modifiers always go last').

options.text: The most emphatic position is always at the end, no matter which sentence pattern you use.
options.whyNot: Tempting because ends are punchy, but only true when the pattern puts the main clause there. In a cumulative sentence the main clause comes first, so the emphasis lands at the start.

options.text: Modifiers always carry the emphasis because they describe things in extra detail.
options.whyNot: Detail is not the same as emphasis. Modifiers add richness, but readers notice where the main clause sits.

options.text: A main clause in the middle always weakens a sentence and should be avoided.
options.whyNot: Too absolute. Middle placement surrounds the main clause with detail, which can add weight and texture; it does not automatically weaken anything.

options.text: Wherever the main clause sits — first, middle, or last — that position is what the reader notices most.
options.whyNot: This survives scrutiny: word order controls emphasis, and the main clause's position is the main lever.

data.scenarioBody: You have 90 seconds to persuade your school to fund a new climbing wall, and you want your very first sentence to keep 600 students leaning forward until the final word. Your speech coach says the opening line should create a little suspense before delivering the point. You could open with the payoff immediately and add detail after, or set two ideas in mirrored opposition — but you want the audience waiting.

targetAnswer.decision: Use a periodic sentence: hold the main clause until the end.
targetAnswer.rationale: A periodic sentence saves the main clause for the end, which builds suspense and delivers a punch — exactly the effect the coach asked for. A cumulative sentence would spend the main clause immediately, killing the suspense; a balanced sentence creates symmetry, not suspense.

blocks.purpose: Retrieve the rhetorical grammar distinction: pick the one defensible statement about when a fragment or unconventional structure is a deliberate stylistic choice versus an error in formal writing.

options.text: A fragment is always an error, even when the writer uses it on purpose.
options.whyNot: Tempting because fragments are usually errors, but rhetorical grammar explicitly allows a deliberate fragment for emphasis — the writer controls the effect.

options.text: A fragment is acceptable only when the writer uses it deliberately, with control, and the context makes the emphasis clear.
options.whyNot: This one survives scrutiny: a deliberate, controlled fragment used for emphasis is a stylistic choice, while anything accidental is an error.

options.text: A fragment is fine anywhere in formal writing as long as it sounds dramatic.
options.whyNot: Dramatic is not a license. Uncontrolled fragments confuse readers and look careless in formal writing.

options.text: A run-on can be left unfixed if the two ideas are closely related.
options.whyNot: Even related ideas need a period, a semicolon, or a conjunction — closeness does not cancel the punctuation problem.

Use a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) — or a semicolon. And a rhetorical fragment only works if it is deliberate and short; an accidental fragment is just an error.

rule.name: Deliberate Structure
rule.statement: Choose each sentence shape on purpose: a periodic sentence saves the main clause for the end to build suspense, a cumulative sentence opens with the main clause and piles on detail, a comma splice is repaired with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction or subordinating word, and a fragment earns its place only when it is deliberate and controlled.

data.scenarioBody: Your school's student newspaper asked you to polish this paragraph for Friday's issue: 'The robotics team worked for six months. They built a robot that could sort recycling. The team won the regional final, it beat eleven other schools. Victory.' The editor wants drama and rhythm, but the writing must stay grammatically clean — no accidental fragments, no comma splices.

targetAnswer.decision: Example rewrite: 'After six months of work, the robotics team finished a robot that could sort recycling — and it won the regional final, beating eleven other schools. Victory.' or, as a periodic version: 'Because they had worked for six months building a recycling-sorting robot, the team swept the regional final, beating eleven other schools. Victory.'
targetAnswer.rationale: The periodic version holds the main clause (the team swept the regional final) until the end so the win lands last; the cumulative version opens with the main clause and adds detail after. The comma splice is repaired with a comma plus 'and' (a FANBOYS conjunction) before 'it won'. The fragment 'Victory.' is deliberate: it is short, controlled, and placed after a complete sentence to emphasize the result, so it is a rhetorical fragment rather than an accidental error.

options.text: Delete the period: 'Fear is a reasonable response to danger panic is not.' — keep it as one flowing sentence.
options.whyNot: This makes the run-on worse. Fusing two complete sentences with no punctuation at all is exactly the error that blurs the argument; the reader crashes into 'panic' with no signal.

options.text: Split it: 'Fear is a reasonable response to danger. Panic is not.' Then add a deliberate fragment if you want extra punch: 'Not panic.'
options.whyNot: Survives scrutiny: it fixes the run-on with a period, restores clear end-focus on 'not', and the optional deliberate fragment adds punch on purpose — the boundary between accident and choice is respected.

options.text: Replace the period with a comma: 'Fear is a reasonable response to danger, panic is not.'
options.whyNot: That's a comma splice — a comma alone can't join two complete sentences, so this is still a run-on, just with a comma painted on top.

options.text: Turn the second half into a fragment: 'Fear is a reasonable response to danger. Panic is not.' but delete 'Panic' so it reads '...to danger. Is not.'
options.whyNot: It deletes the subject 'Panic', leaving 'Is not.' with nothing to refer to — an accidental fragment, not a deliberate one, because the reader can't recover the missing subject.

rule.name: Consistent voice and mood, plus one deliberate pattern
rule.statement: Keep the voice and the mood consistent unless the shift is clearly intentional, and use a rhetorical pattern (parallel structure, periodic order, or cumulative detail) so the sentence persuades, not just reports.

data.scenarioBody: Your class is running the annual museum field trip, and last year's announcement confused everyone. The draft above mixes a statement, a passive construction, a command, and casual slang — and nobody knew what they actually had to do. The principal wants a new announcement of at most two sentences that (1) keeps one voice and one mood throughout, and (2) uses one deliberate rhetorical pattern from rhetorical grammar — a periodic build-up, a cumulative detail pile, or a parallel structure — to make the deadline feel urgent. The facts students need: the bus leaves at 7:30 a.m. sharp, students should pack a lunch, bring a signed permission slip, and arrive ten minutes early.

targetAnswer.decision: Students: before 7:30 a.m. on trip day, pack a lunch, sign your permission slip, and arrive ten minutes early — because the bus leaves at 7:30 sharp, and it will not wait.
targetAnswer.rationale: I kept the voice active throughout (students pack, sign, arrive; the bus leaves) and the mood consistent (imperative-style directive wrapped in indicative statements), so there is no unmarked shift. The parallel list 'pack a lunch, sign your permission slip, and arrive ten minutes early' builds rhythm and makes the demands feel official, and end-focus puts the urgent fact — the bus will not wait — in the last position, where readers remember it.

targetAnswer.decision: A camera was found near the gym entrance on Tuesday, and it has not been claimed. The principal requested that it be returned to the front office by Friday.
targetAnswer.rationale: The camera (the receiver) is the point of the story and the finder is unknown or unimportant, so passive voice (was found, has not been claimed) is the deliberate, correct choice for the lead. blocks.purpose: Confront the #1 error from this unit — the belief that passive voice and subjunctive forms are always mistakes — by making the learner pick the one statement that survives scrutiny among tempting flawed options.

options.text: Passive voice is always a grammar error, so every passive sentence should be rewritten in active voice.
options.whyNot: Tempting because teachers often ask you to cut weak passives, but passive voice is a deliberate choice: it's correct when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or when you want to emphasize the receiver of the action.

options.text: Subjunctive forms like 'If I were' are mistakes; you should always use 'If I was' because that's what people say.
options.whyNot: Tempting because everyday speech often uses was, but were is the standard subjunctive form for hypotheticals and wishes, and 'that he be' is standard in formal demands.

options.text: Both passive voice and subjunctive mood are intentional choices a writer makes for emphasis or tone, and each becomes an error only when a sentence shifts into it without a purpose.
options.whyNot: This survives scrutiny: voice and mood are authorial tools, not errors. A shift is only inappropriate when it happens by accident or confuses the reader.

options.text: Any sentence that changes voice or mood midway is automatically wrong and must be split in two.
options.whyNot: Tempting, but shifts are perfectly fine when they're intentional and clear. Only accidental, unannounced shifts hurt the writing.

rubric.label: No confused words, fragments, or run-ons

data.scenarioBody: You are writing a short appeal for the town newsletter. A walking trail behind the middle school has been damaged by litter, but nobody knows who left the trash there, and the town council cares more about the trail itself than about catching anyone. Twelve student volunteers have offered to help, but no adult supervisor has been assigned yet, and the council wants volunteers to sign up ahead of time. The council's office has asked you for a formal two-sentence appeal for the front page: one sentence that emphasizes the trail and its condition rather than whoever littered it, and one sentence that states the council's request in formal language.

rule.name: Voice and mood are deliberate choices
rule.statement: Use active voice when the doer and energy belong up front; use passive voice when the doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant and the receiver or action is the point. Use the subjunctive (were, that it be) for wishes, hypotheticals, and formal demands. Avoid commonly confused words (like its/it's and affect/effect), and make sure every sentence is complete — no fragments, no run-ons.

targetAnswer.decision: The trail behind the middle school was littered with trash, and the mess has spread along nearly a mile of the path. The council requested that volunteers be signed up by Friday so the cleanup can begin on time.
targetAnswer.rationale: The trail (the receiver) is the point of the first sentence, and whoever littered it is unknown or unimportant, so passive voice — was littered — is the deliberate, correct choice. The second sentence states a formal demand, so it takes the subjunctive: requested that volunteers be signed up, not 'are signed up'. Both sentences have their own subject and verb, no confused words slipped in, and neither is a fragment or a run-on.

checks.prompt: Turn this active sentence into passive voice, keeping the same information: 'The principal handed the trophy to Rivera.' Which version is the correct passive?
checks.answer: The trophy was handed to Rivera by the principal.
checks.rationale: Forming the passive: the object (the trophy) becomes the subject, and the verb becomes a form of be plus a past participle (was handed), with the doer moved into a by-phrase.
checks.hint: The new subject becomes the receiver of the action, and the verb becomes be plus a past participle.
choices: The principal was handed to Rivera by the trophy.
The trophy was handed to Rivera by the principal.
The trophy handed the principal to Rivera.
Rivera handed the trophy was to the principal.
checks.focus: Formation and emphasis: turning an active sentence passive and naming what each voice emphasizes

checks.rationale: The subjunctive uses were — not was — in if-clauses about unreal or hypothetical situations.
checks.hint: For a hypothetical about yourself, the subjunctive swaps a common verb form for an unusual one.

If I were the coach, I would start you.
If I am the coach, I would start you.

blocks.purpose: Confront the #1 misconception — that passive voice is always an error — by making the learner pick the sentence where passive is the deliberate, correct choice.

options.text: "Passive voice is always bad writing. Every sentence you write in the passive voice is an error you should fix."
options.whyNot: Tempting because teachers flag a lot of lazy passive sentences. But passive voice is a choice, not a crime. Writers use it on purpose when the receiver of the action matters more than the doer, or when the doer is unknown.

options.text: "Twelve laptops were stolen from the lab overnight. Anyone with information is urged to come forward."
options.whyNot: This one survives. The doer is unknown, so active voice would have to invent or dodge a subject. Passive puts the stolen laptops — the thing readers care about — in the spotlight. This is the deliberate, correct use of passive.

options.text: "The essay was being written by me, and then it was being edited by me too, and it was being finished late."
options.whyNot: Tempting because it looks formal and grammatical. But nothing here needs passive: the doer (me) is known and the active verbs 'I wrote, I edited, I finished' would be shorter and stronger. This passive just pads the sentence.

rule.name: Voice matches emphasis
rule.statement: Choose active voice when the doer of the action deserves the spotlight; choose passive voice when the receiver of the action, or the action itself, matters more than who did it.

data.scenarioBody: You intern at a water-quality lab. Overnight, one of your coworkers mixed up two sample labels — an honest mistake. The samples were rerun and everything passed. Your supervisor needs to email the client a one-sentence status update tomorrow morning. The client mainly wants to know: are the results trustworthy? The supervisor also does not want the email to name and shame the intern, though the intern is a known person. Decide which voice the sentence should use, then write the sentence itself.

targetAnswer.decision: Passive voice, for example: "A labeling error was corrected and all samples were rerun; every result now meets the required standards."
targetAnswer.rationale: The rule says to pick the voice that puts the right thing in the spotlight. The client's real question is whether the results are trustworthy, so the samples and the passing results — the receivers of the actions — deserve the emphasis. Passive voice ('was corrected', 'were rerun') keeps the focus on the tests and their outcome while letting a known doer stay out of the spotlight. Active voice would make the intern the subject and turn a reassurance into a blame report.

blocks.purpose: Plausible flawed options that tempt the #1 error (semicolon where a colon is needed), so the learner must justify the correct mark against the intuition that failed.

options.text: Semicolon
options.whyNot: Tempting because semicolons feel 'fancier' than commas. But a semicolon must join two complete sentences. Here, only the first half is complete; the second half is just a list, so the semicolon has nothing to join.

options.text: Comma
options.whyNot: A comma could legally connect these, but it gives the list no punch. When you want the reader to sit up and wait for what comes next, a stronger mark is the better choice.

options.text: Colon
options.whyNot: This survives every test: the words before it form a complete sentence, the words after it are a list being introduced, and the colon builds the pause that gives the list its punch.

options.text: Dash
options.whyNot: A dash could set off the list, and it would sound loud. But a dash is for surprise or an abrupt break. This list is a calm, planned buildup, not a jolt, so the colon fits the rhythm better.

misconception.detail: An ellipsis shows the voice trailing off or words left out — it cannot replace a period or question mark at the end of a complete statement. Also check your voice: an announcement written in passive voice ('All club members are asked to...') sounds official and cold. Active voice with a dash or ellipsis gives you the hesitant tone.

data.referenceNote: Rules you may lean on: ellipsis = trailing off, never a substitute for a period or question mark; dash = sharp emphasis; active voice = the doer does the verb.

rule.name: Punctuation sets the tone
rule.statement: Identical words read differently depending on the mark: a comma gives a mild pause, a dash gives a sharp emphasis, and an ellipsis lets a thought trail off — but an ellipsis never replaces a needed period or question mark, and one pause point takes one mark.

data.scenarioBody: Maya wrote a text announcement for the school's recycling drive: "Every student must bring one plastic bottle to room 12 by Friday. No exceptions." Her club advisor says the message sounds bossy. Maya wants the same facts — one bottle, room 12, Friday — but a tone that trails off gently, as if she's shy about asking, not ordering. She wants to keep it in active voice and use at most one special mark.

targetAnswer.decision: For example: "Could you maybe bring a plastic bottle to room 12 by Friday... just one is enough?"
targetAnswer.rationale: The ellipsis mid-sentence makes the voice trail off and sound hesitant, but the sentence still ends with its needed question mark. The sentence stays in active voice (the student does the bringing), and only one special mark is used at the pause point.

blocks.purpose: Tempting flawed options about when an ellipsis can end a sentence, forcing learners to reject using an ellipsis in place of a needed period or question mark and to recall the four-dot rule.

options.text: Use three dots: the ellipsis ends the sentence, so no period is needed.
options.whyNot: Tempting because an ellipsis looks like it can stand in for a period — but an ellipsis never replaces needed end punctuation. Without the fourth dot, the reader can't tell the sentence actually ended.

options.text: Use two dots, since the ellipsis is 'half a sentence' here.
options.whyNot: An ellipsis is always three dots for trailing off or omission. Two dots isn't a punctuation mark anyone uses.

options.text: Drop the ellipsis and use just a period — the omission isn't important.
options.whyNot: If the writer wants to show words were left out, the ellipsis is required. Dropping it hides the omission from the reader.

options.text: Use four dots: three for the omission plus a period to end the full sentence.
options.whyNot: Correct. The omission takes three dots, and a full sentence ending at the omission still needs its period — so four dots total.

blocks.purpose: Targets the #1 mistake for this age: swapping a hyphen (-) for a dash (—) or piling up multiple marks at one pause point, showing why intuition fails.

choices: I was going to tell you —
I was going to tell you-
I was going to tell you: —
I was going to tell you... —
data.commonErrorLabel: Hyphen standing in for a dash
data.context: "I was going to tell you—" she stopped suddenly, embarrassed.
data.correctReasoning: Choice 0 uses a real dash (—), the long mark, right where her words cut off. A sharp interruption gets exactly one mark, and a dash is the mark built for it: it shows the sentence broke off abruptly, without needing a period or anything stacked after it. The hyphen in choice 1 is too short and wrong for the job, and choice 3 piles two marks on one pause.
data.question: The interruption is cut off sharply. Which line punctuates it correctly?
data.recoveryTip: Before you write a dash, picture the long line: —. If what you typed is short like a minus sign, you wrote a hyphen. And one break gets one mark — never stack punctuation.

trapReasons.1: A hyphen is the shortest mark and joins compound words like well-known; it can't carry a sharp break, though it's the character people reach for by habit.
trapReasons.3: Stacking an ellipsis and a dash puts two marks at one pause point — the overuse error.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: On a keyboard, the hyphen is the easiest key to hit, so it becomes the stand-in for a dash. But a hyphen (-) only glues words together, like in well-known or mother-in-law. A dash (—) is a longer mark that signals a sharp break or interruption. They are different marks with different jobs, and stacking an ellipsis plus a dash breaks the one-mark-per-pause rule.

data.scenarioBody: You edit the school paper, which follows AP style. Your friend Maya submits a blurb for the news section: 'The debate team — winners of three straight meets — will compete Saturday, and, if they win again, they'll head to the state finals.' Your editor flags two things: AP style prefers commas over dash pairs for mild, non-emphatic asides like this one, and the blurb piles up pauses ('Saturday, and, if...') where one mark per pause point should do. Maya also asks whether the split infinitive in her other draft, 'to fully support the team,' is an error that AP will reject.
data.scenarioTitle: Editing Maya's Blurb for the School Paper

targetAnswer.decision: The debate team, winners of three straight meets, will compete Saturday, and if they win again they'll head to the state finals. The dash pair becomes a comma pair because the aside is mild, and the double pause after 'Saturday' is trimmed to one comma. 'To fully support' can stay: AP treats split infinitives as a convention choice, not an error.
targetAnswer.rationale: AP style is a convention-setter, not a rule about absolute correctness. The aside 'winners of three straight meets' is non-emphatic, so it needs commas — the dash pair is for sharp breaks or emphasis. The stacked pauses violate one mark per pause point, so 'and, if they win again,' loses its extra comma. And the split infinitive is a disputed usage that guides settle by convention — no absolute error, so it stands.

It declares absolute right and wrong for every rule in English, settled once and for all.
It only lists vocabulary words and their dictionary definitions.
It replaces the dictionary and decides which new words are officially real.
checks.focus: What a style guide is and what it does and does not settle

checks.prompt: Which disputed rule has changed most over time, going from something editors loudly criticized to something most now accept?
checks.answer: The use of hopefully to mean 'I hope that', once attacked, now widely accepted
checks.rationale: The deciding fact is the shift over time: hopefully was once called an error but is now broadly accepted, while the other choices have stayed stable style-guide disagreements.
accepts: An introductory word writers may place a comma after in some guides
checks.hint: Three of these choices are punctuation or word-order rules; one is a single word whose meaning shifted over time.
choices: A comma placed before the final item in a series, required by one guide and optional in another
Starting a sentence with a conjunction like And, banned in one guide and allowed in another
Ending a sentence with a preposition, forbidden by some editors and fine to others
The use of hopefully to mean 'I hope that', once attacked, now widely accepted
checks.focus: Matching each disputed rule (Oxford comma, split infinitive, singular they, hopefully) to its status

checks.prompt: A sentence reads: 'The debate ended the editor finally agreed.' What is the real problem with this sentence?
checks.answer: It is a run-on sentence — two independent clauses fused with no punctuation between them.
checks.rationale: The deciding fact is the grammar structure: two complete independent clauses are joined with no punctuation or conjunction, which is a run-on, not a disputed style choice.
accepts: It is a run-on; two independent sentences are joined with no punctuation
checks.hint: Check each part: can each half stand alone as a full sentence, and is anything connecting them?
choices: It is a split infinitive, a disputed style choice that some guides allow.
It is a fragment, because the second part has no subject.
It is a run-on sentence — two independent clauses fused with no punctuation between them.
It is correct in AP style but wrong in Chicago style.
checks.focus: Disputed rules vs. outright errors

checks.prompt: Type the correct word: 'The new style guide will ___ every article we publish.' Is 'The pilot was late the takeoff was delayed' a fragment or a run-on? Answer with the missing word first, then fragment or run-on (for example: word, run-on).
checks.answer: affect, run-on
checks.rationale: The deciding facts: affect is the verb meaning to influence, so it fits after 'will' and before the object; 'The pilot was late the takeoff was delayed' fuses two independent clauses with no punctuation, so it is a run-on.
checks.hint: Affect is usually the verb (to influence); effect is usually the noun (a result).
checks.focus: Confused word pairs (affect/effect) and fragment vs. run-on identification

checks.prompt: Which of these is a genuine error, not just a difference between style guides?
checks.answer: 'She asked for the vote and every student raised a hand and the chair counted them.'
checks.rationale: The deciding fact is that run-on sentences are grammatical errors under every style guide, while the other options are disputed choices that guides answer differently.
accepts: They are two independent clauses joined by and with no comma
checks.hint: Style-guide choices change from one guide to another; a real error breaks grammar in every guide.
choices: 'Chicago adds a comma before the final item in a series; AP leaves it out.'
'Hopefully, the meeting will end on time, according to most modern editors.'
'She asked for the vote and every student raised a hand and the chair counted them.'
'We split the infinitive to boldly list the rules, and our guide allows it.'
checks.focus: Spotting the genuine error vs. a mere style-guide difference

checks.prompt: An editor tells you their style guide now allows singular they in formal articles. In a short phrase, explain why style guides revise rules like this.
checks.answer: Usage changes over time, and guides follow how people actually write rather than freezing old rules.
checks.rationale: The deciding fact is that disputed rules change over time because usage shifts; guides are updated to match real writing, not the reverse.
checks.hint: Ask what happened with hopefully and with singular they: did the rule change, or did English itself change?
checks.focus: Applying a style guide to an editorial decision and explaining why conventions change over time

plans.approach: Balanced mix: about half typed/cued-recall and cloze items, a third multiple choice for close-option discrimination, and the rest error-spotting or compare/fix tasks — matching the level's blueprint proportions. Styles rotate (plain, scenario, data, error_spot, compare, interest-free since no stated interests) so no skill is tested the same way twice; difficulty stays fair to each slot's fixed lev

layout.context: easy: identify whether a short example is a fragment (missing subject or verb), plain style
easy cloze: commonly confused pair (their/there/they're), type the right word in a sentence
easy: pick the fix for a comma splice (period, semicolon, or comma+FANBOYS)
easy cloze: its/it's — type the correct form to complete a sentence
easy scenario: student's draft sentence, decide fragment or complete sentence
medium cloze: affect/effect — type the correct word in a short science-class sentence
medium: identify a run-on (fused sentence) vs correctly punctuated version, choose the diagnosis
medium cloze: than/then — type the correct word in a sequence-of-events sentence
medium error_spot: worked sentence containing one run-on or splice error to find and fix
medium cloze: your/you're — type the correct form in a friendly note context
medium: choose the best fix for a subordinate-clause fragment (because/when opener), two fix options compared
medium cloze: whose/who's — type the correct word in a question or clause
hard error_spot: short paragraph draft with a fragment and a comma splice; identify and correct both, explain briefly
hard: discriminate among close confusables (accept/except or principal/principle) in a formal sentence, multiple choice
hard: given a run-on with two clauses, choose the fix that best preserves meaning (semicolon vs period vs FANBOYS), comp

0.prompt:
Is this a fragment or a complete sentence?

"Down the middle of the empty hallway at midnight."
0.answer: It's a fragment — it has no subject or verb.
0.rationale: There is no subject and no finite verb, so it is a fragment.
choices: It's a fragment — it has no subject or verb.
It's a fragment — it has no verb.
It's a complete sentence.
It's a run-on sentence.

1.prompt:
Type the correct word to complete the sentence.

The actors forgot ____ lines during the first rehearsal.
1.rationale: The lines belong to the actors, so the possessive "their" is correct.

2.prompt:
This sentence has a comma splice. Which version fixes it correctly?

"The bakery smells amazing, we stopped for croissants."
2.answer: The bakery smells amazing, so we stopped for croissants.
2.rationale: A comma splice needs a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, or a semicolon/period; only comma + "so" works here.
choices: The bakery smells amazing, so we stopped for croissants.
The bakery smells amazing we stopped for croissants.
The bakery smells amazing, we stopped for croissants.
The bakery smells amazing; so we stopped for croissants.

3.prompt:
Type the correct word to complete the sentence.

The puppy wagged ____ tail when the door opened.
3.rationale: "Its" is the possessive form; "it's" means "it is," which does not fit.

4.prompt:
Maya wrote this in her draft: "Because the bus arrived twenty minutes late."

Is it a fragment or a complete sentence, and why?
4.answer: Fragment — there is no main verb.
4.rationale: A clause starting with "because" is dependent, so it has no finite main verb and is a fragment.
choices: Fragment — there is no main verb.
Fragment — there is no subject.
Complete sentence.
Fragment — it does not express a complete thought even though it has a subject and verb.

5.prompt:
Type the correct word to complete the sentence from a science class.

Fertilizer can ____ how fast the bean plants grow.
5.rationale: "Affect" is the verb meaning to influence; "effect" is usually a noun.

6.prompt:
Which diagnosis fits this sentence?

"The thunder rolled closer we packed up the tents quickly."
6.answer: Run-on — two complete sentences are joined with no punctuation.
6.rationale: Two independent clauses are fused with no punctuation between them, so it is a run-on (not a splice, which needs a comma).
choices: Run-on — two complete sentences are joined with no punctuation.
Comma splice — two sentences joined only by a comma.
Correctly punctuated sentence.
Fragment — it is missing a verb.

7.prompt:
Type the correct word to complete the sentence about a sequence of events.

We finished the poster first, and ____ we cleaned up the glue and scissors.
7.rationale: "Then" shows time order; "than" is used for comparisons.

8.prompt:
Find and fix the error in this sentence. Type the corrected sentence.

"The power went out during the storm we lit candles."
8.answer: The power went out during the storm, so we lit candles.
8.rationale: Two independent clauses are fused; adding a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (or a period/semicolon) fixes the run-on.
accepts: The power went out during the storm, so we lit candles.
The power went out during the storm. We lit candles.
The power went out during the storm; we lit candles.

9.prompt:
Type the correct word to complete this friendly note.

____ the best study partner I've ever had — thanks for the help!
9.rationale: The sentence means "you are," so the contraction "you're" is correct; "your" shows possession.

11.prompt: At lost-and-found, the teacher holds up a jacket and asks, "Does anyone know __________ jacket this is?" Type the correct word.
11.rationale: "Whose" shows possession (the jacket belongs to someone). "Who's" is a contraction of "who is," which makes no sense here: "who is jacket this is?"

12.prompt: Find the error in each sentence and name it. Sentence 1: "Although the gym was crowded, and the line was long." Sentence 2: "Mia finally reached the front, she had waited twenty minutes." Type your answer like this: 1: (error), 2: (error)
12.rationale: Sentence 1 has a subordinating word (although) but no complete main clause, so it is a fragment. Sentence 2 joins two independent clauses with only a comma, which is a comma splice.

14.prompt: Which fix best keeps the close, cause-and-effect connection between these two ideas in one sentence? "The storm knocked out the power the whole street went dark."
14.answer: The storm knocked out the power; the whole street went dark.
14.rationale: The two clauses are closely related, so a semicolon joins them in one sentence and keeps the connection; the other choices either splice with a comma, bury the link with an added clause, or lose the tight link.
choices: The storm knocked out the power, the whole street went dark.
The storm knocked out the power; the whole street went dark.
The storm knocked out the power. The whole street went dark, because it was nighttime.
The storm knocked out the power, so the whole street went dark and the neighbors lit candles and the dogs started barking.

plans.prompt:
Style guides disagree about plenty of "rules": the Oxford comma, split infinitives ("to boldly go"), singular they, starting sentences with "hopefully." Defenders say language changes and clarity is what matters. Critics say the old rules keep writing precise. So who decides how we should write?

Write a 4–6 paragraph essay arguing your position on ONE disputed rule of your choice. To make your case, you must put the tools from this cycle to work:

1. Explain the debate: what the rule says, and show it with a real example sentence of your own.
2. Give the strongest argument on BOTH sides — the defenders' and the critics' — before you answer them. (This is a good place for a conditional or subjunctive sentence: "If the rule were dropped..." / "I wish critics would admit that...")
3. Use voice on purpose: write at least one sentence in the passive voice where the passive actually helps you, and be able to say why.
4. Use punctuation for effect at least three times: a dash for a sharp break or emphasis, a colon to introduce a list or explanation, and a semicolon to join two closely related sentences.
5. Somewhere in the essay, address the real question: style guides settle these disputes, not absolute right and wrong — so whose style guide should win, and why?

Aim for about 400–600 words. It is marked against the rubric below and passes at 75%; below that you revise it with the feedback and hand it in again. Write honestly, mark the spots where you made a deliberate choice (you can put a brief note in brackets, like [passive on purpose] or [dash]). You will get feedback with strengths and next steps.
plans.guidance: Take a firm side, prove it with real examples of the rule in sentences, and use dash, colon, semicolon, and voice or mood on purpose to make the essay read the way you want it to.

criteria.name: Argument and use of taught grammar
levels: The essay takes a position but never supports it, or drifts between sides — a reader finishes without knowing why the rule is or isn't needed, and the grammar tools are never mentioned at all.

The essay states a position and gives one example of the rule in use, but the explanation stays shallow (it just says the rule is 'good' or 'outdated') and no voice, mood, or pause-punctuation choices are shown on purpose.

The essay explains the debate clearly: it shows what the rule does in a real example, weighs both sides, takes a firm position, and uses at least one taught tool (active/passive voice, conditional or subjunctive mood, or a dash/colon/semicolon for effect) with a purpose the reader can see.

The essay argues a clear position with well-chosen examples of the rule in real sentences, deliberately contrasts voice or mood to show different effects (for example active for accusation, passive for uncertainty), uses dash, colon, or semicolon to control rhythm, and directly answers the 'who decides?' question using what style guides actually do.

criteria.name: Word choice: the right word, not the near-miss
levels: Confused words (affect/effect, its/it's, their/there/they're, fewer/less) are misused several times, including affect/effect, and no difficult words are used in a way that shows their meaning.
One or two confused-word errors remain, and word choice is mostly plain, with little evidence that any richer vocabulary was chosen to fit the topic.
Confused pairs are used correctly, including affect/effect used properly in the argument, and at least a few precise words fit their context (for example 'prescribe' the rule, 'imply' a judgement).

Confused pairs are handled flawlessly and the word choice is deliberately precise — vocabulary is chosen for its exact meaning and shown in context so a reader could infer each new word's sense from the sentence around it.

criteria.name: Structure: the essay is shaped, not just typed
levels: Paragraphs are hard to tell apart, ideas repeat or jump around, and punctuation marks are piled on (dashes and ellipses everywhere) so the emphasis feels random.
A beginning, middle, and end exist, but paragraphs mix several ideas, transitions are missing, and pause punctuation is overused — a dash or comma appears at nearly every pause point.

Each paragraph covers one clear move in the argument, transitions guide the reader between them, and dash, colon, semicolon, and comma are each used where their effect fits (colon after a complete sentence to introduce, semicolon between related sentences, dash for a sharp aside).

The essay's shape carries the argument: an opening that frames the debate, a paragraph per point, and a closing that lands the verdict, with pause punctuation used sparingly and precisely so each dash, colon, or semicolon earns its emphasis and no mark is wasted.

criteria.name: Clarity: the reader never has to reread
levels: The writing is hard to follow: vague pronouns, buried points, and sentences that must be reread leave the argument unclear.
The point usually comes through, but some sentences are wordy or ambiguous, and the reader occasionally has to work out who or what is being discussed.
Sentences are generally clear and direct, using active voice where it helps and passive only on purpose, so the reader can follow each step of the argument without rereading.

Every sentence says exactly what it means on first reading — voice is chosen to match the emphasis wanted, conditions and hypotheticals ('if the rule were dropped...') read smoothly, and the reader never has to guess the point.

criteria.name: Vocabulary used in real context
levels: Vocabulary is missing or copied in awkwardly, so quoted words sit strangely in the sentence and their meanings never come through.
One or two key terms are used with a roughly correct meaning, but others are forced in or defined flatly instead of being shown in use.
Key terms are woven naturally into sentences where their meaning is clear from context, and the argument relies on at least two of them used accurately.

Key terms are handled like a writer who owns them: each appears in a context that makes its meaning obvious, subtle differences between terms (for example 'mood' vs 'voice', 'style guide' vs 'rule') are respected, and at least one term is used in a fresh way that sharpens the argument.

questions.prompt: A writer argues that the town should build a public skate park. Which objection most directly challenges the proposal?
choices: The town should also repair several cracked streets.
Skateboarding equipment can be expensive for beginners.
Building the park would require replacing the community soccer field.
Many teenagers prefer watching films to outdoor activities.
questions.explanation: Replacing the soccer field identifies a specific cost of the proposal and therefore directly challenges it.
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: A writer claims that a library tool-lending program helps families avoid buying tools. Program records show that participants borrow tools they would otherwise have purchased. Which sentence best explains how this evidence supports the claim?
choices: Some power tools are more expensive than hand tools.
Participants are required to return borrowed tools within two weeks.
Borrowing a tool can replace buying one, so participating families save the purchase cost.
The library’s repair workshop is busiest on Saturday mornings.
questions.explanation: Borrowing a tool instead of purchasing one shows how the program produces the claimed savings.
questions.skill: Explaining the Link Between Evidence and a Claim
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: A writer argues that the school board should start lunch periods 30 minutes later. Which sentence presents the strongest counterclaim to that position?
choices: Later lunches could leave too little time for students to travel to after-school jobs or activities.
Some students say they prefer the current lunch schedule.
The cafeteria serves lunch on twelve separate lines.
A recent article discusses how families plan school-day meals.
questions.explanation: The objection predicts a concrete disadvantage—less travel time for after-school commitments—that directly challenges starting lunch later.
questions.skill: Identifying a counterclaim to an argument
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer says, “If the city adds benches along a walking trail, residents will walk on it more often because resting will be easier.” Which sentence most clearly states the writer’s testable prediction?
choices: A trail survey found that many walkers bring water bottles.
The city already places benches beside two lakes.
Residents often use sidewalks instead of trails on weekend mornings.
Adding benches along the trail will cause residents to walk it more often.
questions.explanation: This sentence is the writer’s testable prediction because it connects adding benches with an increase in walking.
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: Which source is most useful for determining whether a community center's after-school program reduces unsupervised time outdoors?
choices: A program report describing weekly activities, schedules, staff roles, and available resources.
A newspaper report presenting one parent's opinion that the program appears enjoyable.
A district report quoting an editorial that supports building more recreational spaces.
A research report comparing observed outdoor activity before and after the program opened.
questions.explanation: Direct observations before and after the program provide evidence about the behavior the writer's claim addresses, while the other sources do not.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A city council is considering replacing diesel buses with electric buses on Route 8. Which source would best test whether the change would reduce pollution without raising operating costs?
choices: A transit-agency report comparing emissions and operating costs on comparable diesel and electric bus routes
A transit-agency report comparing passenger wait times on routes that use diesel and electric buses
A manufacturer brochure comparing the purchase price and battery range of several electric bus models
A rider survey asking whether Route 8 passengers would prefer electric buses
questions.explanation: This source directly measures both pollution and operating costs under comparable transit conditions, making it the strongest test of the proposed change.
questions.skill: Selecting evidence relevant to a claim
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Which source would provide the strongest evidence for the position that community colleges should offer more evening classes to accommodate students who work during the day?
choices: Faculty surveys showing which class times instructors prefer to teach
Campus transit schedules showing when buses connect to major employers
Tuition comparisons showing community colleges cost less than four-year universities
Enrollment records showing unmet evening-course demand among students who work during the day
questions.explanation: Enrollment records showing unmet demand among students who work during the day directly connect the proposed solution to the needs identified in the position.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A city installed traffic signals at a busy crosswalk. Afterward, average vehicle speed on that block fell from 28 miles per hour to 19 miles per hour. Which statement best explains how the evidence supports the claim that the signals may slow traffic?
choices: The crosswalk may cause more pedestrians to visit the downtown block.
The city may have reduced the speed limit when the signals appeared.
The lower speed measurements after installation are consistent with drivers slowing near the signals.
Two marked pedestrian crossings already serve traffic on the busy block.
questions.explanation: The measured drop in speed after installation directly connects the signals with slower vehicle travel.
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Rhetorical Analysis — Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Before using a poll to measure support for a new city park, a researcher wants to word the question neutrally. Which question is best for that purpose?
choices: Don't you think the new park would make families safer and improve the neighborhood?
Do you support or oppose the proposed city park?
Most residents want a new park, don't they?
How much do you personally enjoy spending time in the city's parks?
questions.explanation: The second question asks for a position without loaded praise or an assumed majority, so it measures support neutrally.
questions.skill: Avoiding bias in questions used as evidence
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Which sentence states a position on an issue?
choices: The city should plant more trees along its busiest sidewalks.
Summer temperatures were 3 degrees cooler near large shade trees.
Residents who walk downtown often carry water during hot weather.
A city survey asked residents which public spaces they visit.
questions.explanation: This sentence states a clear, arguable recommendation about how the city should develop its sidewalks.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A report finds that students attending free after-school tutoring earn higher grades than students who do not attend. Which conclusion is best justified?
choices: The program guarantees higher grades for every student who attends three sessions each week.
Students who skip tutoring sessions are generally less motivated to succeed in their courses.
Free tutoring will raise student grades in every school that adopts the same program.
The program may improve grades, but the report alone does not prove that attendance caused the difference.
questions.explanation: The observed grade difference supports a cautious possibility but does not by itself establish causation or guarantee the same results elsewhere.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a concession to acknowledge an opposing view while defending the writer's position?
choices: Although some residents worry about the cost, the program would give many more students access to tutoring.
Many students need help with coursework, so the district should expand tutoring.
The tutoring program costs less each year than the district originally projected.
Residents have expressed concern about the proposed tutoring program.
questions.explanation: The first clause acknowledges the cost concern, while the second clause defends the program by explaining its benefit.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A pilot program gives students ten minutes of quiet time before each test. Early results show fewer skipped questions. Which sentence states a conclusion that the evidence supports without overstating it?
choices: Early results prove that the program eliminates skipped questions.
Early results may indicate that the program reduces skipped questions.
The program is designed to make students finish every test question.
Quiet time is common in elementary classrooms.
questions.explanation: The cautious wording connects the early results to the program while acknowledging that the finding is not final or absolute.
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Rhetorical Analysis — Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A town wants to decide whether expanding its composting program would reduce household trash. Which source offers the strongest evidence?
choices: A city report comparing weekly trash totals before and after composting expanded
A food blog post describing why home composting benefits the environment
A school flyer advertising a community compost giveaway day
A store advertisement comparing prices for different compostable bags
questions.explanation: The report's before-and-after measurements directly test whether the program is associated with lower trash totals.
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Rhetorical Analysis — Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer argues that the library should stay open on Sundays because most people who visit libraries do so on weekends. Which evidence would most strengthen this argument?
choices: A survey found that 68 percent of library visitors visit on Saturdays or Sundays.
A survey found that 68 percent of library visitors visit on weekdays.
A report found that the library's Sunday hours cost as much as its Saturday hours.
A report found that nearby bookstores close on Sundays.
questions.explanation: The survey showing that most library visitors come on weekends directly supports the claim that Sunday opening would serve the people who use the library.
questions.skill: Choosing evidence that strengthens an argument
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: Which sentence presents the strongest counterclaim to the position that all public libraries should extend their evening hours?
choices: The library currently closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays and weekends.
Some evening visitors use public computers to complete job applications.
Extending library hours might require reducing staff or services during the day.
Local taxes help fund free library programs for children and adults.
questions.explanation: It identifies a possible staffing or service cost of extending hours, directly opposing the proposed policy.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer argues that the school should require students to wear uniforms. Which response most effectively answers the objection that buying uniforms creates financial strain for some families?
choices: The school could provide clothing vouchers and accept donated uniforms.
Many students say they prefer wearing their own clothes.
The school has offered dress-code suggestions for years.
Uniform styles change more often than other school clothing.
questions.explanation: Providing vouchers and donated uniforms directly addresses families' inability to afford required clothing.
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Rhetorical Analysis — Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Which sentence states a central claim rather than supporting evidence?
choices: A study tracked students' sleep duration and course performance for one school year.
The study measured sleep in hours and test scores on a four-point scale.
Students who get regular sleep may perform better in demanding courses.
The researchers recorded each student's sleep and grades every Friday.
questions.explanation: This sentence presents the arguable position that regular sleep may improve performance, while the other choices report details from a study.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer argues that the public library should lend laptops to students who cannot use school devices. Records show that 27 students who cannot use school devices and have no internet access at home borrowed library laptops and completed online homework. Which sentence best explains how the record supports the position?
choices: Most students who need a laptop are unable to complete assignments at school.
Lending laptops gives students who lack a school device and home internet a way to complete online homework.
The program will ensure that every student finishes all online homework.
Library laptops are used more often for research than for homework.
questions.explanation: The record shows that lending laptops lets students who lack a school device and home internet complete online homework, directly supporting the proposal.
questions.skill: Explaining how evidence supports a position
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Which investigation would provide the strongest evidence for the claim that adding a daily reading period improves reading proficiency?
choices: A school compared its students' reading scores before and after adding a daily reading period.
A study randomly assigned classes to a daily reading period or the usual schedule and compared reading gains.
A survey asked students how much they enjoy reading during a daily reading period.
A review summarized how several schools structure their daily reading periods.
questions.explanation: Random assignment and a comparison group better isolate the reading period's effect on reading gains than the other designs.
questions.skill: Evaluating evidence for a causal claim

questions.prompt: A school board proposes replacing printed course schedules with an online catalog and says every student will be able to access course information equally. Which statement most directly challenges that claim?
choices: Students without reliable internet access may miss updates that the printed schedules would have provided.
Students who prefer printed materials may find the online catalog less convenient to use.
Students who already use online calendars may need less help navigating the catalog.
Students in advanced courses may meet with counselors more often to review their options.
questions.explanation: Limited internet access could prevent some students from receiving timely course information, directly challenging the board's claim of equal access.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A survey of 420 high school students found that 58 percent of students who exercised three times a week reported lower stress than before they began exercising. Which conclusion is best supported without going beyond the survey's evidence?
choices: The survey links regular exercise with lower reported stress among the students studied but does not establish causation.
Regular exercise causes lower stress among all high school students, regardless of other conditions.
Students who exercise three times a week will remain free from high stress throughout their lives.
Regular exercise has no relationship with stress among the high school students who responded.
questions.explanation: The survey supports an association among the students studied, but its design does not justify a general causal claim.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer claims that requiring bicycles to have front and rear lights would make night rides safer. Which finding offers the strongest direct evidence for that claim?
choices: A survey found that many cyclists replace their light batteries only once a year.
A study of night crashes found that cyclists with working lights were involved in fewer crashes than cyclists without them.
A survey found that most local bicycle shops sell lights for between $8 and $15.
A poll found that 71 percent of local residents support requiring bicycle lights.
questions.explanation: The crash study directly links working bicycle lights with fewer night crashes, which supports the claim that requiring lights would make night rides safer.
questions.skill: Selecting direct evidence for a claim

questions.prompt: Which piece of evidence most directly supports the position that cities should make public transportation free for students?
choices: City leaders disagree about how to fund student transit passes.
A city report found that fare-free student passes increased transit use by 18 percent.
Students who travel without paying may face fines when inspectors board.
Some students can already receive discounted passes through their schools.
questions.explanation: The measured increase in ridership provides concrete evidence that fare-free passage can encourage transit use among students.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer takes the position that the city should replace its oldest bus shelters with weatherproof ones. Which finding gives the most direct support for that position?
choices: At the two oldest shelters, 38 of 45 daily riders reported waiting in rain or snow last winter.
The city replaced 12 bus shelters with glass models during a downtown renovation in 2019.
Riders at four newer shelters often carry umbrellas while waiting for buses in wet weather.
The transit agency maintains about 140 bus shelters across the city and its suburbs.
questions.explanation: The rider reports directly show that the oldest shelters expose users to rain or snow, which supports replacing them with weatherproof shelters.
questions.skill: Selecting evidence that directly supports a position
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer wants to argue that sugary drinks should not be sold in schools. Which source would be the most credible evidence about how often students drink sugary drinks?
choices: A blog post by a parent claiming that her child drinks soda every day.
A school nurse's survey of 300 students about their drink choices during the week.
A soda company's report stating that most students prefer water.
A social media poll asking followers whether they drink soda.
questions.explanation: The nurse's survey gathers information from many students about their actual drink choices, making it more credible than an anecdote, a self-selected poll, or a claim from a company with a stake in the outcome.
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: A survey of students at one urban middle school finds that 80 percent prefer digital textbooks. Which conclusion is best supported by the survey?
choices: Students at similar urban middle schools may also prefer digital textbooks.
All middle school students across the country prefer digital textbooks.
Digital textbooks are more popular with teachers than with parents.
Rural middle school students strongly prefer printed textbooks.
questions.explanation: Because the survey covers one urban middle school, it supports a cautious conclusion about similar schools rather than a nationwide claim.
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: A city proposes replacing a paved plaza with trees. A council member objects that the plaza hosts weekend markets. Which reply most effectively responds to that objection?
choices: The city could reserve one side of the plaza as permanent market space.
Trees would make the downtown area cooler during summer.
Weekend markets currently draw a large number of shoppers.
The plaza was paved before the nearby park was built.
questions.explanation: Reserving space for the markets directly addresses the council member's concern about losing the plaza's existing use.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer argues that starting classes 30 minutes later would mean fewer buses arrive late and fewer students miss class. Which statement supplies the unstated assumption needed to reach that conclusion?
choices: Students who arrive before class begins are more likely to attend it.
Students generally prefer shorter bus rides over shorter mornings.
Bus routes with fewer stops usually have more late arrivals.
Schools often reward students who arrive before the bell.
questions.explanation: The argument needs the premise that arriving on time makes students more likely to attend class in order to connect fewer late buses with fewer missed classes.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer argues that the town should add a covered bicycle lane. A reader objects that the lane would take away parking spaces. Which sentence offers the strongest rebuttal?
choices: A traffic study found that most downtown drivers arrive before the morning rush.
A design review found that covered bicycle lanes can improve the appearance of a street.
A parking study found enough unused spaces in a nearby garage to replace every space the proposed bike lane would remove.
A resident survey found that some drivers would prefer more bicycle access downtown.
questions.explanation: By showing that every removed parking space could be replaced by an existing unused space, this option directly answers the concern about a net loss of parking.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A researcher randomly assigned students to type essays daily or keep their normal writing routine. Students who typed daily made fewer spelling errors. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: The random assignment supports a causal effect of daily typing on spelling accuracy.
The random assignment proves that typing was the only cause of every improvement.
The random assignment shows that all students improved by exactly the same amount.
The random assignment demonstrates that every student began with identical writing habits.
questions.explanation: Random assignment makes preexisting participant differences less likely to explain the result, supporting a causal effect of daily typing on spelling accuracy.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Which source would provide the strongest evidence for the position that riders who use city scooters should be required to wear helmets?
choices: A medical study comparing head-injury rates among helmeted and unhelmeted scooter riders
A survey asking helmet manufacturers which safety features they prefer
An opinion poll asking city residents whether they dislike helmets
A newspaper editorial claiming that helmets are inconvenient to wear
questions.explanation: The medical study directly connects helmet use with the outcome the position seeks to reduce.
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Rhetorical Analysis — Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer argues that the town should add crossing guards near the middle school because drivers may not slow down for children crossing the street. Which sentence best explains why the proposed solution could improve safety?
choices: Crossing guards could slow traffic and help children cross the road safely.
The school route passes two streets with heavy morning traffic.
Many families walk together because they enjoy the conversation.
The crossing guard program would require two new employees.
questions.explanation: Crossing guards could slow traffic and help children cross the road safely, directly explaining how the proposal might reduce danger.
questions.skill: Explaining how evidence supports a position
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A school measures playground surface temperatures and finds them to be 12 degrees Celsius lower in areas shaded by trees. Which inference most directly supports a proposal to plant more trees around the playground?
choices: Tree shade lowers surface temperature, so more trees could make recess areas cooler.
Tree roots may disrupt nearby paving, adding a maintenance burden to the project.
Dense branches may reduce teachers' visibility across crowded play areas.
Some students may choose quieter games when more of the playground is shaded.
questions.explanation: The measured temperature difference supports the causal link between shade and cooler playground surfaces.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A student wants to know whether a longer library orientation reduces first-time users' difficulty using the catalog. Which study would provide the strongest evidence?
choices: New users choose either a 20-minute orientation or the usual 5-minute introduction, and the librarian rates how confident each group feels afterward.
Experienced library staff complete a 20-minute orientation and then try the catalog under timed conditions.
New users are randomly assigned to a 20-minute orientation or the usual 5-minute introduction, and researchers compare the number of catalog errors in both groups.
Two new users try the catalog after one orientation, while two other new users try it without any orientation.
questions.explanation: Random assignment and a common error measure provide the clearest test of whether the longer orientation causes fewer catalog mistakes.
questions.skill: Comparing research designs for evidentiary strength
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Which finding would provide the strongest research evidence that secure parking could encourage bicycle commuting?
choices: A commuter survey found that 64 percent of respondents would ride more often if secure parking were available.
A commuter survey found that 28 percent of respondents already ride a bicycle to work regularly.
A station survey found that most train riders arrive by bus or on foot.
A neighborhood survey found that 71 percent of residents want more trees along the main street.
questions.explanation: The finding directly measures stated willingness to cycle more after secure parking becomes available, so it supports the claim with research evidence.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer argues: "Because our town's recycling rate rose after it added curbside pickup, the town should add curbside pickup to every neighborhood." What unstated reasoning connects the evidence to the claim?
choices: Curbside pickup makes recycling easier for residents.
Most residents already know which materials can be recycled.
Recycling bins are cheaper to buy than compost bins.
Other towns have received complaints about missed pickups.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that making recycling easier will raise participation, and that unstated reasoning is what connects the observed increase to the recommendation.
questions.skill: Identifying the warrant in an argument
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: Two surveys ask students whether they want longer lunch periods. One survey included 15 students, and the other included 1,500 students. Which conclusion best follows from this information?
choices: The smaller survey is more reliable because every student's answer was counted.
The larger survey is more reliable because its larger sample is less likely to reflect only a few unusual preferences.
The smaller survey is more reliable because it took less time to complete.
Both surveys are equally reliable because they asked the same question.
questions.explanation: A sample of 1,500 students is less likely than a sample of 15 to be skewed by a few unusual preferences, so the larger survey gives the more reliable estimate.
questions.skill: Judging the strength of evidence by sample size
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: A writer argues that schools should add 15 minutes to physical education because students will spend more of the day being active. Which finding most directly supports the argument?
choices: Health guidelines recommend that children get 60 minutes of physical activity each day.
A student survey found that many students enjoy participating in team sports.
Coaches at schools with longer PE periods reported greater student participation.
PE activity logs at schools with longer class periods showed more time spent in moderate-to-vigorous activity.
questions.explanation: The activity logs directly connect longer PE periods with more time spent in moderate-to-vigorous activity.
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: Which statement makes a verifiable claim about what a public library does rather than an evaluation of how well it serves patrons?
choices: The library stays open until 9 p.m. on weekdays.
The library's evening program is the most popular program it offers.
The library's evening program is more useful than its weekend program.
The library's evening program is more valuable to students than other city services.
questions.explanation: A library's weekday closing time is a factual statement that can be verified against its published schedule.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A district wants to determine whether replacing diesel buses with electric buses would reduce roadside pollution. Which investigation would provide the strongest evidence?
choices: Ask drivers whether electric buses are quieter than diesel buses.
Compare the maintenance costs of electric buses and diesel buses.
Rotate electric and diesel buses across the same routes on comparable days and measure exhaust pollutants.
Interview transit workers about which type of bus performs best.
questions.explanation: Rotating the two bus types across the same routes on comparable days and measuring exhaust pollutants provides the strongest direct test of whether electric buses reduce roadside pollution.
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Rhetorical Analysis — Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A city is considering adding bicycle-route signs. Which result would most strongly support the idea that the signs increase bicycle use?
choices: Bicycle counts rose on signed routes after installation and also rose on comparable unsigned routes.
Bicycle counts fell on signed routes after installation but stayed about the same on comparable unsigned routes.
Bicycle counts rose on signed routes after installation but stayed about the same on comparable unsigned routes.
Bicycle counts rose on signed routes before installation but stayed about the same on comparable unsigned routes.
questions.explanation: Only the signed routes showed a post-installation increase while comparable unsigned routes did not, making the signs the most plausible cause.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer claims that a school garden teaches students how food grows. Which detail offers the clearest support for that claim?
choices: The garden's website explains which students may join its weekly planting and harvesting club.
Students who tended the garden correctly identified the growth stages of the vegetables they planted.
Students who tended the garden said that the garden looked especially colorful in the spring.
A local article describes the school garden as a pleasant outdoor classroom for students.
questions.explanation: Correctly identifying growth stages demonstrates the garden's instructional effect more directly than describing appearance, participation, or general appeal.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A history club wants to argue that the town's old market hall should be preserved. Which source would provide the strongest evidence for its historical significance?
choices: A state historical survey identifying the hall as a rare surviving example of an early-1900s public market
A travel blog describing the hall as one of the town's best places to eat
A contractor's estimate of the cost to repair the market hall's roof
An online poll showing that many residents want the building preserved
questions.explanation: A state historical survey offers expert research that directly establishes the market hall's historical importance.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Which detail is most useful as evidence for the position that phones should be stored away during class rather than only silenced?
choices: Most students report checking their phones between classes each day
The school policy requires every phone to remain powered off during lessons
Phone batteries generally last longer when brightness settings are lowered
A study found that silenced phones still produce notifications during class
questions.explanation: The finding shows that silencing phones may not prevent classroom notifications, which directly supports storing them away.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: Which sentence best combines a clear position with relevant evidence about later school start times?
choices: Because buses are often delayed by heavy morning traffic, the district should move the first bell to 8:30 a.m.
Buses are often delayed by heavy morning traffic near the high school each morning.
The district moved the first bell to 8:30 a.m. after a traffic study was completed.
A later first bell would help students, although some families may prefer an earlier start.
questions.explanation: The sentence states a recommendation to move the first bell and gives the traffic problem that supports it.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A student is writing an argument that the town should build more playgrounds. Which sentence offers evidence for that position rather than an opinion or a restatement of the claim?
choices: Playgrounds are fun and give children a place to play.
A survey found that 48 percent of local families said they would use a new playground within a mile of their home.
The town should build more playgrounds so children have somewhere to play.
Building playgrounds would make the town a better place to live.
questions.explanation: The survey result gives measurable information about how many families would use a new playground, so it functions as evidence rather than an opinion or a restatement of the claim.
questions.skill: Distinguishing evidence from opinion and claim
questions.topic: Tester 4 of 9: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9

questions.prompt: A city argues that installing permeable pavement will reduce street flooding. Which statement best explains why that solution could work?
choices: The pavement can be installed on streets with several different widths.
Water can pass through openings in the pavement and be absorbed by soil below the road.
Engineers have compared the costs of several available paving materials.
Residents have complained that some streets flood during heavy rain.
questions.explanation: Permeable pavement allows water to enter the soil, which explains how the pavement could reduce the amount of water flowing through streets.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A writer argues that the city should require every apartment building to provide secure bicycle storage. A tenant objects that the requirement could raise rents. Which response most effectively answers the objection?
choices: Apartment residents should stop complaining about every new city rule.
Bicycles cost more to store than cars in most apartment buildings.
The apartment building already has more parking spaces than bicycle spaces.
The city could offer landlords a storage grant so the added cost does not have to be passed on to tenants.
questions.explanation: A storage grant directly addresses the tenant's cost concern by reducing the expense the landlord would otherwise pass on.
questions.topic: Entry Check, Part 4 of 9: Position and Evidence

questions.prompt: A student wants credible evidence about whether free museum admission would increase visits by local teenagers. Which source would provide the strongest evidence?
choices: A university study comparing teenage museum visits before and after admission became free
A survey of museum visitors asking whether they would visit more often if entry were free
An article describing the museum's current exhibits without reporting visitor data
A collection of social media posts from teenagers about a recent museum trip
questions.explanation: A university study comparing teenage visits before and after the change provides direct research evidence about the claim.
questions.topic: Rhetorical Analysis: Concepts through Argument Writing: Position and Evidence

feedback.correct: Good sow — your marble lands with purpose, like a claim backed by solid evidence.
feedback.incorrect: That pit slips through your fingers — remember, a strong position needs the right evidence behind it.
feedback.win: Your store overflowed — you argued your position and the evidence captured the board.
feedback.lose: The board got swept before your argument could land. Review position and evidence, then sow again.
